Medieval historians recorded that ‘Umar consulted the Companions and ‘Ali advised him to go. He appointed ‘Ali to run Madinah in his absence and travelled to Syria.

Accounts, which are later reports and cannot all be verified, say that ‘Umar entered the city riding a camel with a single servant, switching turns. When he arrived at the outskirts, it was the servant’s turn, so he led the animal on foot through a stream and mud. Abu ‘Ubaydah is said to have told him that the commanders and the people of the city would be watching him. ‘Umar replied that Allah had given them honour through Islam and they should not seek it elsewhere.
The detail is typical of the way the early sources describe his character: stern about display, and plain.

‘Umar gave the people of Aelia a written covenant. According to al-Tabari, it said: "This is what the servant of Allah, ‘Umar, the Commander of the Believers, has given to the people of Aelia of safety. He has given them safety for themselves, their property, their churches and their crosses, the sick and the healthy, and all of their community. Their churches will not be inhabited by Muslims, nor destroyed, nor will they be diminished..."

The text, as transmitted, also required them to pay the jizya, the tax paid by non-Muslim citizens in return for protection and exemption from military service, and to send out the Byzantine soldiers and bandits, who would be safe until they reached their destination. Al-Tabari’s text also records a clause, which the people of the city asked for, that Jews would not settle in Aelia. Historians discuss the exact wording and later additions, but its core is a guarantee of safety and religious freedom for the city’s Christians.

It is reported that the patriarch invited ‘Umar to pray in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. He declined and prayed on the steps outside, saying that if he prayed inside, the Muslims after him might take it as a mosque, saying "‘Umar prayed here." He did not want his action to be an excuse for taking a church from its owners.

He asked about the site of the Temple Mount, which was covered with rubbish, and had it cleared, and a prayer place built there, the beginning of what became the Aqsa Mosque as it is known today. The Qur’an says: "Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes, that you deal kindly and justly with them." (60:8)

facts: Rajab 101 AH, in northern Syria, aged about 39
Called by many scholars the fifth rightly guided caliph

s.h: From a prince to a caliph
t: ‘Umar was a great-grandson of the caliph ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab through his mother, and the son of a governor of Egypt. In his youth he is described as living in luxury, with fine clothes and perfume, and he served as governor of Madinah, where he was liked and consulted the scholars. When his cousin Sulayman was dying, he named ‘Umar as his successor.
It is reported that when he was told of his appointment, he said "Verily to Allah we belong, and to Him we return" and wept, regarding it as a calamity, not an honour.

He had the family’s estates and gifts that had been taken from the public treasury inspected and returned. His wife Fatima, a daughter of the previous caliph, is reported to have given her jewellery to the treasury. He reduced his own stipend and lived modestly, and the reports describe him checking on the people’s conditions himself.

He stopped the practice, begun under earlier caliphs, of cursing ‘Ali from the pulpits on Fridays, and had the preachers recite the verse "Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives" (16:90). It has been recited at the end of the Friday sermon ever since.

New converts from the conquered peoples had been made to go on paying the poll tax. ‘Umar ordered it lifted, and told his governor, as reported: "Allah sent Muhammad as a guide, not as a tax collector." The reports say that the people prospered under his policies.

He sent scholars to teach in remote provinces, and in his reign the first official gathering of the Prophet’s hadith was ordered, because he feared that the knowledge would be lost with the scholars. Abu Bakr ibn Hazm was asked to write down what he could (reported by al-Bukhari in the chapter on knowledge).

Yahya ibn Sa’id, who was sent to collect zakat in North Africa, is reported to have said that he looked for poor people to give it to and found none. In the end he used the money to free slaves (reported by Abu ‘Ubayd in Kitab al-Amwal). Historians treat the account as a sign of how widely the justice of his rule was remembered, though not as a precise record of the economy.
He died in Rajab 101 AH at Dayr Sim’an in northern Syria, after an illness, aged about thirty-nine. It was said that some people thought he had been poisoned, though that cannot be established.

facts: Baghdad, and later Cairo, Cordoba and elsewhere
Caliphs such as Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma’mun
Ibn al-Haytham’s Book of Optics, about 1020 CE
Ibn Sina’s al-Qanun, completed about 1025 CE

t: The translators included Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Nestorian Christian physician who rendered Greek medical works into Arabic through Syriac, and Thabit ibn Qurra, from the Sabian community of Harran, who worked in mathematics. They were paid well, and the patron caliphs are reported to have ordered books to be copied and gathered from across the lands.

Historians debate how much of this took place in one single building called the "House of Wisdom". What is clear is that Baghdad had a large and active community of translators, copyists and scholars in the ninth century.

Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked in the House of Wisdom and wrote a book on calculation by "restoration and balancing" (al-jabr wa’l-muqabala), from which the word algebra comes. His name, in Latin form, gave us the word algorithm. He also wrote on the Hindu-Arabic numerals, which spread to Europe through Arabic books.

Astronomers made tables of the stars and measured the size of the earth. The need to find the direction of the qibla and the times of prayer was one reason the Muslims worked on astronomy and geometry.

Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, a physician in Cordoba who died around 1013 CE, wrote an encyclopaedia of medicine and surgery with drawings of surgical instruments. Ibn Sina, who died in 1037 CE, wrote al-Qanun fi’l-Tibb, the Canon of Medicine, which was taught in Europe for centuries.

Ibn al-Haytham, who worked in Cairo, tested ideas about light and vision through experiments and argued that we see because light enters the eye. His Book of Optics was translated into Latin and read by later European scholars.

Scholars of the time saw their work as part of faith. The Qur’an says: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding" (3:190), and the first revelation commands: "Read in the name of your Lord who created." (96:1)

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever treads a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise" (Sahih Muslim). Many of the great names were also scholars of religion. Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd, for example, wrote on both.

facts: Treaty of Ramla with Richard I, September 1192 CE

t: Salah al-Din’s family came from the town of Dvin and he was born in Tikrit. His father and uncle served Nur al-Din, the ruler of Syria. He went with his uncle Shirkuh to Egypt, which was then ruled by the declining Fatimid dynasty, and when Shirkuh died, Salah al-Din became vizier. In 567 AH (1171 CE) he ended the Fatimid caliphate, and Egypt returned to the Sunni fold.

After Nur al-Din’s death, he took Syria and brought the Muslim lands around the Crusader states under a single rule. Contemporary writers describe him as modest and patient, fond of the Qur’an and the company of scholars.

The Crusader states had held coastal Syria and Palestine since the First Crusade (1099). Truces were broken, and in 1187 the Crusader army marched out under King Guy de Lusignan to relieve the town of Tiberias. They were exhausted by the summer heat and thirst. On 4 July 1187 Salah al-Din surrounded them near the Horns of Hattin and destroyed the army.
The way was open. Over the next weeks, many of the coastal cities fell, and he marched to Jerusalem.

Jerusalem was held by Balian of Ibelin, who threatened to destroy the holy places if no terms were given. After negotiations the city surrendered on 27 Rajab, the anniversary of the Prophet’s night journey according to a common reckoning. A ransom was set for each person: ten dinars for a man, five for a woman, one for a child (as reported by contemporary sources). Many who could not pay were freed by his brother al-‘Adil and by Salah al-Din himself.

Christians were allowed to visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the cross was taken down from the Dome of the Rock. Historians contrast these terms with the killings of 1099, though they also note that some people were left unfreed and sold.

The loss of Jerusalem brought the Third Crusade, led by Richard I of England and Philip II of France. Salah al-Din and Richard fought, and negotiated, and in September 1192 they agreed the Treaty of Ramla, which left Jerusalem under Muslim rule and allowed Christian pilgrims to visit.

Salah al-Din died six months later in Damascus. Ibn Shaddad, his advisor, wrote that he left in his treasury only forty-seven silver dirhams and one gold coin, and no property or land, so that his funeral expenses had to be borrowed.

facts: Musnad Ahmad; its grading is debated

s.h: A city many tried to take
t: Constantinople sat between Europe and Asia on a narrow peninsula with massive land walls and, on the sea side, a chain across the Golden Horn. Muslim armies besieged it in the seventh century under Mu’awiyah, in 717–718 CE, and later under the early Ottomans, such as Bayezid I. The Companion Abu Ayyub al-Ansari took part in one early siege and, according to the reports, died and was buried near its walls.
The Prophet ﷺ said that the city would be conquered. This saying was known to the Ottoman sultans and scholars, who regarded it as a high honour for the commander who would do it.

Mehmed II came to the throne for the second time in 1451. In 1452 he built a fortress, Rumeli Hisari, on the European shore of the Bosphorus to control the strait. He hired a Hungarian engineer, Orban, to cast huge cannon, and gathered an army of some tens of thousands of men.
The siege began in early April 1453. For weeks the defenders under Emperor Constantine XI held the walls against bombardment and assaults.

The chain across the Golden Horn kept the Ottoman fleet out. Mehmed had a road laid across the hill behind Galata, greased with tallow, and hauled dozens of ships overland into the harbour above the chain in a single night. The defenders, who had to spread themselves along the sea walls as well, were stretched.

On 29 May, after a last assault, the walls were breached near the Gate of St. Romanus. The emperor died fighting. Mehmed entered the city. As was usual in the warfare of the time, the city was plundered and many of its people were taken captive; Mehmed ordered the plunder to stop, and some of the captives were ransomed or resettled.

Mehmed was given the title al-Fatih, the Conqueror. He had the church of Hagia Sophia turned into a mosque, and rebuilt Constantinople as the Ottoman capital, bringing in people from across his lands to repopulate it.

He also appointed Gennadios Scholarios as Patriarch of the Orthodox Church and recognised the Church’s authority over its own people, so that the Orthodox Christians of the empire lived under their own leaders. Historians continue to discuss how much the Ottoman state at this period resembled later arrangements, but all agree that the city’s Christians were allowed to remain.

facts: About 29 years, roughly 120,000 km by common estimates

t: Ibn Battuta came from a family of legal scholars in Tangier. He studied the Maliki fiqh, and in 1325 he left to make the pilgrimage to Makkah. On the way he passed through Algiers, Tunis, Alexandria and Cairo, and he met scholars and Sufi teachers in each place. He completed Hajj in 1326, and instead of going home, he continued east.
He travelled with caravans of pilgrims and merchants, using the hospitality of the lodges (zawiyas) and the letters of scholars. He often worked as a qadi, a judge, wherever he settled.

He went on to Iraq and Persia, visited Baghdad, and travelled to Makkah again. He sailed down the East African coast to Mogadishu and Kilwa, then to Anatolia and the Black Sea, where he reached the Golden Horde.
He recorded details of the customs and meals of each place, the beliefs of its people, the behaviour of its rulers, and the way scholars were treated.

He travelled across Central Asia and reached the Indus in 1333. In Delhi, he was appointed a qadi by Sultan Muhammad ibn Tughluq, and he stayed for about eight years. He was sent as an envoy to China in 1341, but his ship was lost, and he went on to the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Bengal. His account of the later parts of his journey eastward is where historians disagree most about what he actually saw.
He returned to Morocco in 1349 and soon travelled again, to Granada, and then across the Sahara to the empire of Mali in 1352–1353, where he described the court of Mansa Sulayman.

The sultan of Morocco asked him to write down his experiences. He dictated them in Fez in 1356 to Ibn Juzayy, a scholar from Granada, who edited the text in elegant prose. The book’s full title is "A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling".

He died in Morocco around 1368–1369. His book was little known outside the Muslim world until it was translated into European languages in the nineteenth century. The Qur’an says: "Proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every distant pass" (22:27).

facts: ‘Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, a blind Companion
In Makkah, early in the mission
He gave the adhan in Madinah with Bilal

t: ‘A’ishah said: "‘Abasa wa tawalla was revealed about Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind man. He came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and began to say, O Messenger of Allah, guide me. And with the Prophet ﷺ there was a man from among the great ones of the polytheists. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ began to turn away from him and attend to the other man, saying: Do you see anything wrong in what I say? He said: No. So it was revealed about this." (Sunan at-Tirmidhi 3331)
The Prophet ﷺ’s hope was understandable: if a leading man of Quraysh accepted Islam, many others might follow. But the one who had come in person to learn was the blind man.

"He frowned and turned away because there came to him the blind man. But what would make you perceive, [O Muhammad], that perhaps he might be purified or be reminded and the reminder would benefit him? As for he who thinks himself without need, to him you give attention. And not upon you [is any blame] if he will not be purified. But as for he who came to you striving [for knowledge] while he fears [Allah], from him you are distracted." (80:1–10)

The words are tender: the Qur’an does not name the blind man at the start but speaks of "the blind man", and addresses the Prophet ﷺ in the third person. Commentators note that the Qur’an says "perhaps he might be purified", leaving the matter to Allah.

The Prophet ﷺ received the reproach and never hid it. It stands in the Qur’an for everyone to read, with a clear message: the Prophet ﷺ only conveys what is revealed to him, even when it corrects him.

The reports say that after this he honoured Ibn Umm Maktum, and would greet him with the words quoted above. Ibn Umm Maktum became a mu’adhdhin with Bilal in Madinah: the Prophet ﷺ said, "Bilal calls the adhan at night, so eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls the adhan" (Sahih al-Bukhari 617). Reports also say that the Prophet ﷺ left him in charge of Madinah when he went out on expeditions.

The surah goes on: "Indeed, it is a reminder; so whoever wills may remember it" (80:11–12). The principle is that the sincerity of the person who comes matters more than their rank. A teacher or da’i should not rush to those with influence while turning away from those who want to learn.
It is also a lesson about how people with a disability are treated. The blind man was to be heard, answered, and respected, and he found a place of service in the community.

facts: Ka’b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah, Murarah ibn al-Rabi‘

t: Ka’b said that he had never been stronger or better off than when he stayed behind from Tabuk; he had two riding camels at the time, which he had never owned before. Whenever the Prophet ﷺ planned an expedition he would keep it secret, but for Tabuk he announced it, because the journey was long and the enemy was great.
Ka’b said he kept intending to prepare, and each day he put it off: "Tomorrow I will prepare, and then I will catch up." Until the army had left and it was too late.

When the Prophet ﷺ returned to Madinah, he went to the mosque, prayed two rak’ahs, and sat. Those who had stayed behind, about eighty men, came with excuses and oaths, and he accepted their outward statements and left their hearts to Allah. Ka’b came, and the Prophet ﷺ smiled the smile of an angry man, and asked: "What kept you back? Did you not purchase a mount?"

Ka’b said: "O Messenger of Allah, if I were sitting with anyone of the people of the world other than you, I think I would escape his anger with an excuse, for I have been given eloquence. But by Allah, I know that if I tell you today a lie that pleases you, Allah will soon make you angry with me; and if I tell you the truth, you will be angry with me, but I hope for Allah’s pardon. By Allah, I had no excuse. I was never stronger or richer than when I stayed behind from you." The Prophet ﷺ said: "This man has told the truth. Get up until Allah decides about you."

The Prophet ﷺ forbade the Muslims to speak to the three. Ka’b said that people changed toward him, and the land itself seemed strange. He went out to the markets and no one spoke to him. He greeted the Prophet ﷺ, and wondered whether he had moved his lips to reply. He climbed over the wall of the garden of his cousin Abu Qatadah and greeted him; he did not reply. When he pressed him with an oath, Abu Qatadah only said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." His eyes filled with tears.

At this time a messenger from the king of Ghassan brought him a letter: "We have heard that your master has treated you harshly. Allah has not made you a place of humiliation and loss. Join us and we will console you." Ka’b said: "This too is a trial," and he took the letter to an oven and burned it. After forty days, the Prophet’s messenger told them to separate from their wives. Hilal’s wife was allowed to serve him as he was old, and Ka’b sent his wife to her family.

On the fiftieth morning, after the dawn prayer, Ka’b was on the roof of his house, in the state Allah had described: "the earth had become narrow for them, despite its vastness, and their own souls had become narrow." He heard a man on Mount Sal’ shouting: "Ka’b ibn Malik, rejoice!" He fell down in prostration.

People ran to congratulate him. He took off his two garments and gave them to the man who brought the news, and borrowed others. He went to the mosque, where the Prophet ﷺ’s face was shining with joy. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Rejoice at the best day that has passed since your mother bore you." Ka’b asked: "Is it from you or from Allah?" He said: "No, from Allah."

Ka’b said: "O Messenger of Allah, as part of my repentance, I will give up all my wealth as charity for Allah and His Messenger." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Keep some of your wealth, for it is better for you." So he kept his share at Khaybar. He said: "Allah saved me because of truthfulness, and part of my repentance is that I shall never speak but the truth as long as I live."

The verses say: "And [He also forgave] the three who were left behind [and regretted] to the point that the earth closed in on them despite its vastness and their souls closed in on them, and they were certain that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned to them so they could repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful. O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful." (9:118–119)

facts: Monday, in Rabi’ al-Awwal (commonly the 12th), the Year of the Elephant, c. 570 CE
Makkah, in the clan of Banu Hashim of Quraysh
‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib, who died before his birth
Aminah bint Wahb, who died when he was about six

s.h: The world he was born into
t: Arabia was a land of tribes with no common ruler. Makkah was its religious and commercial centre because it held the Kaaba, the house Ibrahim and Ismail had built for the worship of one God. By then it had been filled with idols, said to number three hundred and sixty, and the tribes made pilgrimage to it. Quraysh, who guarded the Kaaba and fed and watered the pilgrims, were respected everywhere, and their caravans travelled safely to Yemen in winter and to Syria in summer. The Qur’an reminds them of this favour in Surah Quraysh.

It was also a society where the strong could be cruel to the weak: orphans were cheated of their inheritance, daughters were sometimes buried alive (the Qur’an condemns this in 81:8–9 and 16:58–59), and feuds between tribes could last for generations. A few people, called hanifs, rejected the idols and looked for the religion of Ibrahim.

The year of his birth was remembered because of Abraha’s failed march on the Kaaba, described in Surah al-Fil. Quraysh had been spared by an event they could not explain, which only added to the sense that the Kaaba was protected by a power greater than theirs.
The Prophet ﷺ himself marked the day of his birth: when asked about fasting on Mondays he said, "That is the day on which I was born, and the day on which revelation came to me" (Sahih Muslim).

His father died on a trading journey before the child was born. His grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib, the respected leader of Makkah, chose the name Muhammad, "the praised", a name rare among the Arabs. Following the custom of sending babies to the desert to grow up strong and speak pure Arabic, he was entrusted to Halimah al-Sa’diyyah of Banu Sa’d. The Sira reports that her household’s fortunes improved during his stay.

Sahih Muslim (Anas) reports that when he was a young child, Jibril came, opened his chest, took out a clot and washed his heart in a golden basin with Zamzam water, then restored it. The Companions later saw the mark of the stitching on his chest.

At about six he travelled with his mother Aminah to visit relatives in Madinah. On the way back she fell ill and died at al-Abwa. Umm Ayman, a servant, brought him home. His grandfather took him in with great tenderness, but died two years later. The child was then given to his uncle Abu Talib, who loved him and protected him for the next forty years, though he never accepted Islam.

The Qur’an later turns this history into reassurance: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge? And find you lost and guide you? And find you in need and make you self-sufficient?" (93:6–8).

facts: al-Sadiq al-Amin, the truthful and trustworthy
To Khadijah at about 25, she about 40 (as commonly reported)
Al-Qasim and ‘Abdullah (died young), Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah

t: He worked as a shepherd for others, and later said that every prophet had done so: "Allah did not send a prophet except that he shepherded sheep" (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Companions asked, "And you?" He said, "Yes, I used to shepherd them for a few qirats for the people of Makkah."

The biographies report that at about twelve he travelled with Abu Talib to Busra in Syria, where the monk Bahira saw signs in him and advised Abu Talib to protect him. As a young man he traded between Makkah and Syria and became so well known for honesty that Makkans entrusted him with their goods and called him al-Amin.

In his twenties a number of Makkan clans made a pact at the house of ‘Abdullah ibn Jud’an to defend anyone wronged in Makkah, resident or visitor, and to support the oppressed. It was called Hilf al-Fudul. Years later he is reported to have said that he would not exchange his part in it for red camels, and that if he were called to something like it in Islam, he would answer.

Khadijah bint Khuwaylid was a respected, wealthy merchant. She hired him to take her goods to Syria with her servant Maysarah. On their return Maysarah told her of his honesty and character, and she sent a friend to ask whether he would marry her. His uncles agreed and Abu Talib spoke at the wedding.

They had a very close marriage. He lived with her faithfully for about twenty-five years, and after she died he kept praising her. ‘A’ishah said she never felt as jealous of any wife as she did of Khadijah, because the Prophet ﷺ mentioned her so often (Sahih al-Bukhari).

When he was about thirty-five, a flood damaged the Kaaba and Quraysh decided to rebuild it. When the walls reached the corner where the Black Stone sits, the clans quarrelled about who had the honour of lifting it, nearly coming to blows. An elder suggested they accept the first person to enter the courtyard the next morning. It was Muhammad, and they said, "This is al-Amin; we accept him." He spread his cloak, placed the stone on it, asked each clan’s leader to hold an edge and lift it, and set it in place himself.
The Qur’an notes that he was prepared by Allah long before he was sent: "Say: I have lived among you a lifetime before this. Will you not reason?" (10:16).

facts: The cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nur, near Makkah
A pause in revelation, followed by Surah al-Muddaththir

t: ‘A’ishah describes how it began: "The first sign of revelation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was true dreams in his sleep. He never saw a dream except it came true like the break of dawn." After this he began to love seclusion and used to go to the cave of Hira for several nights of worship, taking provisions, then return to Khadijah for more (Sahih al-Bukhari).

s.h: The night of the first revelation
t: The angel came and said, "Read." He replied, "I am not one who can read." The angel took him and pressed him until he could bear no more, released him and said again, "Read." He replied again, "I am not one who can read." The third time the angel pressed him, then released him and said: "Read in the name of your Lord who created. Created man from a clinging substance. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen. Taught man that which he knew not." (96:1–5)

Allah chose, as the first revelation, a command to read and a reminder that He taught through the pen. This matters: the first Qur’anic word to a community that was mostly unlettered was about knowledge.

He returned home trembling and said, "Cover me, cover me!" When his fear passed, he told Khadijah what had happened and said, "I fear for myself." She answered with certainty: "Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep the ties of kinship, you bear the burdens of the weak, you earn for those who have nothing, you honour the guest and you help those afflicted by calamity."

She took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, an old man who had become Christian and knew the Scriptures. When he heard the account, he said, "This is the ‘Namus’ (the angel) that Allah sent to Musa. I wish I were young; I wish I could be alive when your people drive you out." The Prophet ﷺ asked, "Will they drive me out?" Waraqah answered, "Yes. No man has ever brought what you have brought without being treated with hostility." Waraqah died soon afterwards (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

s.h: The pause and the command to rise
t: Revelation then paused for a period, which grieved him. Later, he said, he heard a voice from the sky and saw the angel sitting on a throne between heaven and earth. Frightened, he went home and asked to be covered. Then came: "O you who covers himself, arise and warn. And your Lord, glorify. And your clothing, purify. And uncleanliness, avoid." (74:1–5) From then on, revelation came continuously (Sahih al-Bukhari, Jabir).
Tradition holds that this took place on the night of Laylat al-Qadr, which the Qur’an says was in Ramadan (97:1, 2:185).

facts: Khadijah, ‘Ali, Zayd ibn Harithah, Abu Bakr
The house of al-Arqam, near Safa
From Mount Safa, after the command of 26:214
Abu Lahab, Abu Jahl and the leaders of Quraysh

t: Khadijah was the first to believe. Of the men, Abu Bakr believed without hesitation, and ‘Ali, then a boy of about ten living in the Prophet’s house, and Zayd ibn Harithah, his freed servant, also accepted. Abu Bakr, a respected and well-liked merchant, then invited his friends. According to the biographies, ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan, al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam, ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf, Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas and Talhah ibn ‘Ubaydillah accepted through him.
The believers met quietly, often in the house of al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam near Mount Safa, where the Prophet ﷺ taught them the Qur’an and the prayer.

When Allah commanded, "And warn your closest kinsmen" (26:214), he climbed Mount Safa and called out a cry used to warn of danger: "O Sabah!" The clans of Quraysh gathered. He asked, "If I told you that a cavalry was coming at you from behind this mountain, would you believe me?" They said, "We have never known you to tell a lie." He said, "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab answered, "May you perish! Is this why you gathered us?" Allah revealed Surah al-Masad about him (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Ibn ‘Abbas).

At first many dismissed it. As the Prophet ﷺ criticised the idols and called for the equality of people before Allah, the leaders became hostile. The Qur’an records the labels they used: sorcerer, poet, madman, liar. Their opposition rested less on doubt than on the threat to their status, since their leadership depended on the pilgrimage economy of the idols.

They tried negotiation. According to the Sira, ‘Utbah ibn Rabi’ah offered him wealth, leadership or kingship in exchange for stopping, and the Prophet ﷺ answered by reciting the opening of Surah Fussilat until ‘Utbah asked him to stop. They also pressed his uncle Abu Talib to restrain him. He is reported to have answered, "O uncle, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left to make me abandon this matter, I would not abandon it until Allah makes it prevail or I perish in it."

facts: The weak and those without tribal protection
The Prophet himself was abused at the Kaaba
The matter will be completed (Khabbab’s hadith)

t: Quraysh used the power of clans. A person with a strong clan was protected, even if not by their own faith. Those without such protection, many of them slaves or foreign-born, were made to pay. Bilal ibn Rabah was taken out at noon, laid on the burning sand with a heavy stone placed on his chest, and told to renounce Muhammad. He answered only, "Ahad, Ahad" (One, One). Khabbab ibn al-Aratt was forced to lie on burning coals until his back fat extinguished them. Sumayyah and her husband Yasir were killed; their son ‘Ammar was tortured and, under duress, said what they demanded while his heart stayed firm, which led to the revelation of 16:106, allowing a believer under compulsion to speak words he does not mean.

Abu Bakr bought and freed Bilal and several others, spending a large part of his wealth to do so. (The details of these tortures come mostly from the early biographies; the Sahih collections confirm the suffering of Bilal, Khabbab and the Prophet himself.)

He was not spared. ‘Abdullah ibn Mas’ud reports that the Prophet ﷺ was praying by the Kaaba when Quraysh leaders, including Abu Jahl, sat nearby. One suggested bringing the intestines of a slaughtered camel and throwing them on his back when he prostrated. They did, and he stayed in prostration until his daughter Fatimah came and removed them. He then prayed against those men by name, and Ibn Mas’ud said he later saw every one of them lying dead at Badr (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

‘Urwah ibn al-Zubayr asked ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr what was the worst thing Quraysh did to him. He described how ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu’ayt wrapped his cloak around the Prophet’s neck and twisted it hard, until Abu Bakr rushed up, pushed him away and said, "Would you kill a man because he says, My Lord is Allah?" (Sahih al-Bukhari).

s.h: What the Prophet told his Companions
t: Khabbab asked the Prophet ﷺ, who was resting in the shade of the Kaaba, "Will you not pray for help for us?" He sat up, his face red, and said: "Among those before you, a man would be seized, a pit dug for him, a saw put on his head and he would be split in two; and iron combs would be used on his flesh, and none of it would turn him from his religion. By Allah, this matter will be completed until a rider travels from Sana’a to Hadramawt fearing none but Allah, and the wolf for his sheep. But you are hasty." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

facts: The 5th year of prophethood (c. 615 CE); a second, larger group followed
Ja’far ibn Abi Talib (for the larger group)
The Negus (al-Najashi), a Christian king of Aksum
‘Amr ibn al-‘As and ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi’ah
The Negus died in 9 AH; the Prophet prayed over him in absentia

t: Quraysh had made life hard for the Muslims who had no clan protection. The Prophet ﷺ told them, according to the Sira, that Abyssinia had a king under whom no one is wronged, and advised them to go there until Allah opened a way. A first group of about a dozen men and women left, including ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan and his wife Ruqayyah, the Prophet’s daughter. A larger group followed, around eighty men plus women and children, led by Ja’far.

Quraysh sent ‘Amr ibn al-‘As and ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi’ah with gifts for the king and his generals, and instructed them to approach the generals first. They told the court that these were foolish youths who had abandoned their people’s religion and followed a new one that neither side knew. The generals urged the king to hand them over.
The king said he would not do so without hearing them. Umm Salamah, who was among the emigrants, narrates what followed (Musnad Ahmad).

The Negus asked, "What is this religion that has made you leave your people?" Ja’far answered: "O king, we were a people in ignorance. We worshipped idols, ate carrion, committed shameful acts, cut family ties and treated neighbours badly. The strong among us oppressed the weak. Then Allah sent us a messenger whose lineage, truthfulness, trustworthiness and chastity we knew. He called us to worship Allah alone and to abandon the stones we and our fathers worshipped. He commanded us to speak the truth, keep our trusts, maintain family ties, treat neighbours well and avoid what is forbidden and bloodshed. He forbade lewdness, false speech, taking an orphan’s property and slandering chaste women."

The king asked him to recite something of what the Prophet brought. Ja’far recited the opening of Surah Maryam. The king wept until his beard was wet, and his bishops wept until their scrolls were wet. He said, "This and what ‘Isa brought come from the same lamp." He told the envoys to leave, returned their gifts and refused to hand over the Muslims.

The next day ‘Amr tried again, saying that they say terrible things about ‘Isa. Ja’far told the king: "We say about him what our Prophet brought: he is the servant of Allah, His messenger, His spirit and His word that He cast to Maryam, the virgin." The king drew a line on the ground with a stick and said, "Between your religion and ours there is no more than this line." (As reported in the Sira and Musnad Ahmad.)

It was the first migration in Islam, and showed the principle that when a believer cannot practise freely, seeking a place of safety is lawful. It also showed the Qur’an’s respect for Maryam and ‘Isa. The Negus later accepted Islam. When he died in 9 AH, the Prophet ﷺ told the Companions that a righteous man had died, and prayed the funeral prayer for him in absentia (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: About three years (c. 616–619 CE), in the Shi’b of Abu Talib
Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib, Muslim and non-Muslim
Abu Talib and Khadijah, in the 10th year of prophethood

t: When it became clear that the Prophet ﷺ would not stop and his clan would not hand him over, the leaders of Quraysh agreed in a written pact to boycott Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib: no marriage with them, no buying or selling, and no dealings, until they surrendered Muhammad. The document was hung in the Kaaba.

The clans withdrew to a ravine owned by Abu Talib. For about three years they suffered hunger so severe that, it is reported, children’s cries could be heard from outside and people ate leaves. Some relatives secretly sent food. It ended when a handful of Quraysh themselves, ashamed of the treatment of their kin, worked to cancel the pact. The Sira reports that the document was found eaten by termites except for the words "In Your name, O Allah."

Soon after, Abu Talib, who had protected the Prophet ﷺ for decades, fell ill. When he was dying, the Prophet ﷺ came to him and said, "O uncle, say La ilaha illa Allah, a word I can plead for you with before Allah." Abu Jahl and another man were present and said, "Will you abandon the religion of ‘Abd al-Muttalib?" Abu Talib’s last words were that he was on the religion of ‘Abd al-Muttalib. The Prophet ﷺ said he would keep asking forgiveness for him until forbidden, and then Allah revealed 9:113 and 28:56: "You do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)
It is among the clearest lessons that even a Prophet cannot make someone believe, however deeply he loves them.

Khadijah died shortly afterwards, according to the Sira, a few weeks later, at about sixty-five. She had been his companion, comforter and financial support for a quarter of a century. Their house had been the one place where he found complete trust. Without his uncle’s protection and without his wife, the Prophet ﷺ faced Quraysh largely alone. The biographers named it the Year of Sorrow.
In the time after her death, he married Sawdah bint Zam’ah, a widow whose husband had died in Abyssinia, and was betrothed to ‘A’ishah, the daughter of Abu Bakr (as reported in the Sira).

facts: Rejected, stoned, and returned under the protection of Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi

t: With Abu Talib gone and Quraysh growing bolder, the Prophet ﷺ looked for a new home for the message. Ta’if was a fertile hill town, home to the tribe of Thaqif, with relatives of his own through marriage. He travelled there on foot with Zayd ibn Harithah and approached its three leading brothers, asking for their support and protection for the message.

One said sarcastically that if Allah had sent him, he would tear the cover of the Kaaba; another said, "Could Allah find no one else to send?"; the third said he would never speak to him again, since if he really was a prophet, he was too important to answer. Then they incited their servants and the town’s young men to throw stones. The Prophet ﷺ was driven out, and the stoning continued until he was bleeding from the legs, with Zayd shielding him and being hurt himself.

Exhausted and wounded, he took shelter in an orchard belonging to the sons of Rabi’ah, where he sat down by a wall. The Sira reports that their servant, a Christian called Addas, brought him a bunch of grapes. When the Prophet ﷺ said "Bismillah" before eating, Addas was surprised, and when asked, said he was from Nineveh. The Prophet ﷺ said, "The city of the righteous man Yunus ibn Matta" and told him that Yunus was his brother, a prophet, as he was. Addas bent down and kissed his head and hands.

‘A’ishah once asked him: "Has there been a day harder for you than the Day of Uhud?" He said: "I have suffered from your people what I have suffered. The hardest was the day of ‘Aqabah (Ta’if), when I presented myself to Ibn ‘Abd Yalil and he did not respond. I left, grieved and dazed, and did not recover until I reached Qarn al-Tha’alib. I raised my head, and there was a cloud shading me, and in it Jibril. He said: Allah has heard what your people said and how they answered you, and has sent the angel of the mountains to you, to do what you wish. The angel of the mountains greeted me and said: O Muhammad, if you wish, I will bring together the two mountains of Makkah over them." The Prophet ﷺ said, "No. I hope that Allah will bring from their descendants people who worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

He could not enter Makkah without protection, since Abu Talib was dead. He sent word to several leaders; one of them, Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi, though not a Muslim, put on his weapons and escorted the Prophet ﷺ into the Kaaba. The Prophet ﷺ never forgot it. After Badr he said that if Mut‘im had been alive and asked him to release the prisoners, he would have freed them for him (Sahih al-Bukhari).

facts: The Sacred Mosque (Makkah) → al-Aqsa (Jerusalem) → the heavens
Scholars differ; the popular 27 Rajab is not established by sound evidence
Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Anas, Malik ibn Sa’sa’ah, Abu Hurayrah)

t: The Prophet ﷺ was brought the Buraq, a white animal, larger than a donkey and smaller than a mule, which took its stride at the limit of its sight. He rode it to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), tied it at the post where the prophets tied theirs, entered the mosque and prayed two rak‘ahs. According to Sahih Muslim, the prophets were gathered and he led them in prayer.
Jibril brought him two cups, one of wine and one of milk. He took the milk. Jibril said: "You have chosen the fitrah, the natural way" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

He ascended through the heavens. At each, Jibril asked for the gate to be opened, and the angels asked, "Who is it?" "Jibril." "Who is with you?" "Muhammad." "Has he been sent for?" "Yes." And they welcomed him. In the first heaven he met Adam; in the second, Yahya and ‘Isa; in the third, Yusuf; in the fourth, Idris; in the fifth, Harun; in the sixth, Musa; and in the seventh, Ibrahim, leaning his back on the Bayt al-Ma’mur, which seventy thousand angels enter each day and never return to it (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

He was taken to Sidrat al-Muntaha, the Lote-Tree of the Boundary, beyond which none passes. Surah al-Najm describes it: "His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress. He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord." (53:17–18)

There, fifty prayers a day were prescribed for his community. On the way back he passed Musa, who asked what had been prescribed. When told fifty, Musa said: "Your community cannot bear it. I tested the Children of Israel before you. Go back and ask your Lord for a reduction." He went back, and it was reduced by some. He kept returning at Musa’s advice until it was five. Musa told him to ask again, but he said: "I am ashamed before my Lord." Then a caller said: "I have enforced My obligation and lightened it for My servants." In another narration: "They are five, and they are fifty in reward; the word is not changed with Me." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

In the morning he told Quraysh, who mocked him. They asked him to describe Bayt al-Maqdis, which he had never visited. He said that it was brought before him, and he described it. Some people who had believed reportedly left the faith, while Abu Bakr, told that his friend claimed this, said, "If he said it, it is true." (As reported in the Sira.)

It came after Ta’if and the Year of Sorrow: when the people of the earth turned away, the One who sent him showed him the greatest signs and gave him the gift of prayer, a daily meeting with his Lord. It also connected the Kaaba and al-Aqsa, and made him the leader of the prophets in prayer, preparing the Qiblah question that would arrive in Madinah.

facts: Six men of Khazraj at Mina (11th year of prophethood)
About twelve men, the next year
Seventy-three men and two women, at night
Aws and Khazraj were worn out by civil war

t: Yathrib (later Madinah) was home to two Arab tribes, Aws and Khazraj, and several Jewish clans. The two Arab tribes had fought a long, bitter series of wars, ending with the Battle of Bu’ath just a few years before. Their leaders were exhausted and looked for someone to unite them. They had also heard from their Jewish neighbours that a prophet was expected.

At Mina in the pilgrimage season, the Prophet ﷺ met six men of Khazraj, recited the Qur’an to them and invited them. They said, "By Allah, this is the prophet the Jews threaten us with. Do not let them beat us to him." They believed and promised to spread the message and return the next year.

The next year twelve men came and pledged at ‘Aqabah. ‘Ubadah ibn al-Samit, one of them, described it: "We pledged not to associate anything with Allah, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill our children, not to slander and not to disobey in what is good. Whoever fulfils it, his reward is with Allah." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The Prophet ﷺ sent Mus’ab ibn ‘Umayr to teach them. The Sira recounts how Mus’ab and Asad ibn Zurarah explained Islam to the leaders of Aws, Sa’d ibn Mu’adh and Usayd ibn Hudayr. When Usayd stormed in with a spear to threaten them, Mus’ab said, "Sit and listen. If you like it, accept; if not, we will stop." Usayd listened, said "This is excellent," and accepted Islam. Sa’d did, and then told his clan, "Speaking to your men and women is forbidden to me until you believe in Allah and His Messenger," and by evening almost all had.

In the following pilgrimage season, seventy-three men and two women from Yathrib, hidden among their non-Muslim fellow pilgrims, slipped out at night to meet the Prophet ﷺ at ‘Aqabah. His uncle al-‘Abbas, not yet Muslim, came to make sure they understood the risk. They pledged to listen and obey in ease and hardship, to spend, to command good and forbid evil, to speak the truth fearlessly, and to protect him as they protected their own families. Al-Bara’ ibn Ma’rur took his hand: "By the One who sent you with the truth, we will protect you as we protect our women." They asked what they would receive. He said: "Paradise." (Musnad Ahmad, Ka’b ibn Malik.) Twelve leaders were chosen among them.

facts: Makkah → cave of Thawr → coastal route → Quba → Madinah
Abu Bakr, his servant ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, guide ‘Abdullah ibn Urayqit

t: After the second pledge of ‘Aqabah the Muslims began slipping away to Madinah. Quraysh realised that if the Prophet ﷺ joined them, he would be out of their reach and have an army behind him. The leaders met in the Dar al-Nadwa. Several ideas were suggested; Abu Jahl proposed that one young man from each clan strike him together, so the blood would be spread among all and Banu Hashim could not fight them all. The Qur’an describes this: "And when the disbelievers plotted against you to restrain you or kill you or drive you out; they plan, and Allah plans, and Allah is the best of planners." (8:30)

‘A’ishah reports that the Prophet ﷺ came to Abu Bakr’s house at noon, a time he never visited, and said that he had been given permission to leave. Abu Bakr asked, "With you, O Messenger of Allah?" "With me." ‘A’ishah said she had never before seen anyone weep from joy (Sahih al-Bukhari).

That night the young men surrounded his house. He told ‘Ali to sleep in his bed under his green cloak and to return the trusts that people had left with him. The Sira reports that he walked out through them reciting the opening of Ya-Sin, and Allah made them unable to see him. He met Abu Bakr and they headed south, the opposite direction from Madinah, and hid in the cave of Thawr.

Abu Bakr’s son ‘Abdullah spent the days in Makkah listening and brought news at night; his daughter Asma’ brought food, tearing her waist-belt in two to tie the provisions; ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah grazed sheep over their tracks to hide them and brought milk. They had hired ‘Abdullah ibn Urayqit, a non-Muslim but trustworthy guide, to meet them with the camels after three nights (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Quraysh offered one hundred camels for the Prophet’s ﷺ capture. Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of Allah, if any of them looked down at his feet, he would see us." The Prophet ﷺ said: "O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whose third is Allah?" (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Qur’an records it: "If you do not aid him, Allah has already aided him when those who disbelieved had driven him out as one of two, when they were in the cave and he said to his companion, Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us." (9:40)

On the road, Suraqah ibn Malik, a tracker, set out to catch them for the reward. As he neared, his horse stumbled and its legs sank into the ground, more than once. He asked for forgiveness, offered provisions and promised to turn others back. The Prophet ﷺ asked only that he keep it secret. Suraqah later became Muslim. The Sira reports that the Prophet ﷺ told him, "How will it be when you wear the bracelets of Khosrow?" and this was fulfilled in the time of ‘Umar. (Sahih al-Bukhari for Suraqah’s horse.)

The Muslims of Madinah went out each morning to the edge of the town waiting for him. One day, a man from the Jews saw them and called, "O people of the Arabs, here is your fortune that you have been waiting for!" The Prophet ﷺ stayed first at Quba, where he built the first mosque of Islam (Qur’an 9:108) and stayed four days. Then he travelled to the town itself on his camel, with people on the rooftops and the girls saying, "Muhammad has come." Each clan asked him to stay with them; he said, "Leave her way, she is commanded," and the camel knelt at the plot where the Prophet’s Mosque stands, beside the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.
The Muslim calendar begins with this migration, set by the Companions in the time of ‘Umar, because it marked the point where the community could live as a community.

facts: On land bought from two orphans, with the Companions carrying the bricks
Muhajirun and Ansar paired as brothers
The Constitution of Madinah (reported in the Sira)
Introduced after Abdullah ibn Zayd’s dream
Changed from Jerusalem to the Kaaba after about 16–17 months (2:142–150)

t: The Prophet ﷺ asked for the price of the land where his camel had knelt. It belonged to two orphans; they offered it as a gift, but he insisted on paying. The mosque was built of mud bricks with palm trunks as columns and palm branches as a roof. He worked alongside the Companions, carrying bricks, and they chanted as they worked (Sahih al-Bukhari). It was far more than a place to pray: it was the courthouse, the school, the council room, the hospital tent and the shelter of the poor. A porch at the back housed the poor and homeless Muslims who came to be known as Ahl al-Suffah.

The emigrants had left their homes and wealth in Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ paired each with a man from the Ansar. The Ansar offered half of their homes, orchards and wealth. Allah praised them: "And those who were settled in the home and in faith before them love those who emigrated to them and find no want in their hearts for what the emigrants were given, and prefer them over themselves, even though they are in need." (59:9)

‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf was paired with Sa’d ibn al-Rabi’, who offered half his wealth and one of his two wives. ‘Abd al-Rahman answered: "May Allah bless you in your family and wealth. Show me the market." He made a profit trading and soon married and became one of the most generous donors in Islam (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Madinah had Aws and Khazraj, who had converted or were converting, and several Jewish clans, as well as people who remained polytheists. The Sira preserves a founding document, often called the Constitution of Madinah, which declared the believers one community, put the Jews under the same protection and obligations of mutual defence, and committed all to defend the city against attack and to settle disputes by referring them to the Prophet ﷺ. Some historians discuss when each clause was written, but its general principle is widely accepted as the basis on which the city was run.

s.h: The call to prayer and the Qiblah
t: The Muslims discussed how to call people to prayer: a bell, a horn, a fire. ‘Abdullah ibn Zayd dreamed of a man teaching him the words of the adhan, and ‘Umar saw the same. The Prophet ﷺ told ‘Abdullah to teach it to Bilal, whose voice was beautiful and strong (Sunan Abi Dawud).

For about sixteen or seventeen months the Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem. The Prophet ﷺ used to look up at the sky longing to turn to the Kaaba. Then Allah revealed: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, so We will surely turn you to a Qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram." (2:144) The change took place during prayer at a mosque now called Masjid al-Qiblatayn, the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs (Sahih al-Bukhari, al-Bara’).

In the second year, fasting in Ramadan was made obligatory (2:183–185), together with zakat al-fitr, and the first Eid prayers were held. When he arrived in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ saw the Jews fasting on the day of ‘Ashura’ in thanks for the rescue of Musa, and said, "We have more right to Musa than you," and fasted it and told the Muslims to do so (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: The wells of Badr, about 150 km south-west of Madinah
14 Muslims martyred; about 70 Quraysh killed and about 70 captured

t: Quraysh had seized the homes and wealth of the emigrants when they left Makkah. News came that Abu Sufyan was returning from Syria with a large trade caravan, guarded by few men, along the road near Madinah. The Prophet ﷺ called the Muslims to intercept it, saying whoever has a mount ready should come. Many stayed behind because they did not expect a battle.

Abu Sufyan learned of the plan, took the caravan along the coast and sent a rider to Makkah for help. Quraysh marched out with their army under Abu Jahl. Abu Sufyan’s caravan escaped, and he sent word that they need not fight, but Abu Jahl insisted on going to Badr, feasting and drinking.

When news came that an army, not a caravan, was ahead, the Prophet ﷺ asked for advice. Abu Bakr and ‘Umar spoke well. Then al-Miqdad ibn ‘Amr stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah, go where Allah commands you; we are with you. We will not say as the Children of Israel said to Musa, ‘Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are staying here.’ Rather, go, you and your Lord, and fight, and we are fighting with you." (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Prophet ﷺ was looking for the answer of the Ansar, since their pledge at ‘Aqabah was to protect him in Madinah, not abroad. Sa’d ibn Mu’adh stood and said: "If you led us into this sea, we would plunge in with you; not one of us would stay behind. We are patient in war and sincere in battle." The Prophet ﷺ was delighted and said: "March on, and be glad."

Allah sent rain that night. It firmed the sand beneath the Muslims and turned the ground beneath Quraysh to mud, and gave them a light sleep that took away their fear: "[Remember] when He covered you with drowsiness, security from Him, and sent down upon you from the sky rain to purify you and remove from you the evil of Satan and to bind your hearts and plant firmly thereby your feet." (8:11)

The Prophet ﷺ spent the night praying beneath a tree. In the morning he lined up the ranks and made a long dua: "O Allah, if this band of Muslims is destroyed today, You will not be worshipped on the earth." He stretched out his hands until his cloak fell from his shoulders, and Abu Bakr put it back, saying, "Enough, O Messenger of Allah, you have implored your Lord urgently, and He will fulfil what He promised you." (Sahih Muslim)

It began with single combat. Three Makkan champions, ‘Utbah, Shaybah and al-Walid, challenged the Muslims. Three Ansar stepped forward, but they said they wanted their own cousins. The Prophet ﷺ sent Hamzah, ‘Ali and ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, and the first two quickly killed their opponents and helped ‘Ubaydah, who was wounded and died later (as ‘Ali narrates, Sahih al-Bukhari).

In the general fighting the Muslims prevailed; the Qur’an says angels fought with them: "When you asked help of your Lord, and He answered you: I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another." (8:9) Abu Jahl was struck down by two young Ansar, Mu’adh ibn ‘Amr ibn al-Jamuh and Mu’awwidh ibn ‘Afra’, and ‘Abdullah ibn Mas’ud found him dying and finished him (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Seventy were taken captive. The Prophet ﷺ asked Abu Bakr and ‘Umar. Abu Bakr suggested ransom, since they were kin and the money would strengthen the Muslims, and ‘Umar suggested execution. He inclined to Abu Bakr’s view. The next day Allah revealed 8:67–68 in the direction of ‘Umar’s stricter view, that it was not for a prophet to take prisoners until he had established his authority; but the ransom was allowed (Sahih Muslim). Prisoners were to be treated well; some were reportedly freed in exchange for teaching ten Muslim children to read and write (Musnad Ahmad).

The Muslims who fought at Badr were afterwards given great honour. When ‘Umar wanted to punish Hatib ibn Abi Balta’ah for sending a letter to Quraysh before the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ said: "He took part in Badr. How do you know that Allah has not looked at the people of Badr and said: Do what you will, for I have forgiven you?" (Sahih al-Bukhari).

facts: The mountain of Uhud, north of Madinah
About 70, including Hamzah and Mus’ab ibn ‘Umayr

t: Quraysh wanted revenge for Badr, in which many of their leaders had died. They raised an army of about three thousand, with their wives to urge them on, and camped at Uhud. The Prophet ﷺ had a dream in which a cow was slaughtered and his sword was notched, which he interpreted as losses among his companions, and he preferred to defend inside Madinah. But the younger men who had missed Badr wanted to go out and fight, and he agreed. When he had put on his armour, many regretted having pressed him, but he said: "It is not for a prophet, once he has put on his armour, to take it off until Allah judges between him and the enemy." (Musnad Ahmad)
On the way, ‘Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites, withdrew with about three hundred men, saying, "He listened to the youths and did not listen to me." (3:166–167)

The Prophet ﷺ lined up the army with the mountain at their backs and placed fifty archers under ‘Abdullah ibn Jubayr on a hill, with the instruction: "Protect us from behind. If you see us seized by birds, do not leave your place until I send for you. If you see that we have defeated the enemy and trampled them, do not leave your place." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The Muslims began to push the enemy back, and the Makkans broke and fled, leaving their camp. When the archers saw the spoils, most said, "The battle is won; take the spoils." Their commander reminded them of the order, but many went down. Khalid ibn al-Walid, then still with Quraysh, saw the gap, rode around the hill and attacked from behind.

In the chaos, someone shouted that Muhammad had been killed. The Prophet ﷺ was struck by a stone, his lower right tooth was broken and a helmet ring was driven into his cheek. He fell into a pit dug by the enemy. Sahl ibn Sa’d described it: his face was wounded, his front tooth broken and his helmet smashed on his head. Fatimah washed the blood while ‘Ali poured water; when she saw that the water only made it bleed more, she burned a piece of a woven mat and pressed the ash onto the wound until the bleeding stopped. (Sahih al-Bukhari)

A small group stayed to protect him, including Abu Talhah, who shielded him with his body, Talhah ibn ‘Ubaydillah, Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas, and Nusaybah bint Ka’b (as reported in the Sira). Ka’b ibn Malik recognised the Prophet ﷺ and shouted to the Muslims that he was alive, and the believers rallied around him.

About seventy Muslims were killed. Hamzah, the Prophet’s uncle and "the lion of Allah", was killed by Wahshi, an Abyssinian slave who had been promised freedom for killing him; the Prophet ﷺ was deeply grieved at the sight of his body (Sahih al-Bukhari). Mus’ab ibn ‘Umayr, who carried the banner, fell too. Anas ibn al-Nadr, who had missed Badr, fought until his body had over eighty wounds, and could be identified only by his sister by his fingertips (Sahih al-Bukhari).

As the Makkans left, Abu Sufyan called from the mountain: "Is Muhammad among you?" The Prophet ﷺ told them not to answer. Then he asked about Abu Bakr and ‘Umar. Finally he shouted, "These have been killed! If they were alive, they would have answered." ‘Umar could not hold himself: "You lie, O enemy of Allah! Allah has kept alive what will shame you." Abu Sufyan said: "A day for a day: war goes by turns." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Al ‘Imran 3:121–179 discusses Uhud in detail, and its tone is mercy: "Do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are [true] believers. If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the others. And these days We alternate among the people." (3:139–140) It names disobeying the order as the cause (3:152), yet adds "He has already pardoned you" (3:152). And it describes those who, despite their wounds, responded to the call to pursue the enemy the very next day, at Hamra’ al-Asad: "Those to whom the people said, The people have gathered against you, so fear them; but it increased them in faith, and they said, Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." (3:173)

facts: Quraysh, Ghatafan and other tribes: about 10,000 men
A trench across the northern, open side of Madinah

t: After Banu al-Nadir, a Jewish tribe expelled from Madinah for plotting against the Prophet ﷺ, settled in Khaybar, their leaders travelled among the Arab tribes urging them to join Quraysh in a single decisive campaign. Roughly ten thousand men arrived outside Madinah, a force far beyond anything the city had faced.

Madinah is protected by lava fields and houses on most sides; the open side is north. Salman al-Farisi, who knew how Persian cities were defended, is reported to have suggested a trench. The Muslims dug it within days, in the cold, many of them hungry. The Prophet ﷺ dug alongside them and carried earth until his belly was covered in dust. When they chanted, he chanted with them: "O Allah, there is no good except the good of the Hereafter, so forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirun." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah saw the Prophet ﷺ with a stone tied to his belly because of hunger and, going home, asked his wife what food they had. They had a small goat and a little barley. He invited the Prophet ﷺ quietly, but the Prophet called all the diggers, about a thousand. He blessed the pot and bread, and everyone ate until they were full, and the pot was still boiling with meat and the dough was still being baked as before (Sahih al-Bukhari).

The Arab armies arrived to find an obstacle they had never seen, which the horses could not cross. They camped in front of it and exchanged arrows for weeks. A few of their horsemen found a narrow point to cross, and ‘Ali killed ‘Amr ibn ‘Abd Wudd, their champion, in single combat (Sira).

The worst blow was inside the city. Banu Qurayza, a Jewish tribe bound by the Constitution of Madinah to defend it, were persuaded by Huyayy ibn Akhtab of al-Nadir to break the treaty and allow the army to attack from the south. The Qur’an describes the fear: "When they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah [various] assumptions." (33:10)

The Prophet ﷺ prayed: "O Allah, Revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, defeat the confederates. O Allah, defeat them and shake them." (Sahih al-Bukhari). Na’im ibn Mas’ud, a newly Muslim man unknown to the besiegers, sowed distrust between Quraysh and Qurayza (Sira). Then Allah sent a cold wind that overturned their pots and tents and troops, and "an army you did not see" (33:9). Abu Sufyan ordered a retreat. The Prophet ﷺ said: "From now on we will march against them and they will not march against us." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The Muslims then besieged Banu Qurayza for about twenty-five days. They surrendered and asked that their allies from Aws arbitrate; the Prophet ﷺ appointed Sa’d ibn Mu’adh, a leader of Aws. Sa’d judged that the fighting men be killed, the women and children taken and the property divided, a judgement the Prophet ﷺ said was in accord with Allah’s judgement (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). This is a difficult passage of the Sira. It was a wartime judgement on a tribe that had betrayed the city during an existential siege, delivered by their own chosen arbitrator, and it should be read in that context and not as a general rule.

facts: About 1,400, unarmed except for travel swords, with sacrificial animals
Al-Hudaybiyyah, at the edge of the sacred territory

t: The Prophet ﷺ saw in a dream that he was entering the Sacred Mosque and performing the rites. He announced it and set out with about fourteen hundred men, wearing the ihram and driving seventy sacrificial camels, to show clearly that they came for worship and not war. Quraysh sent out cavalry under Khalid ibn al-Walid to stop them, so the Prophet ﷺ took a rough mountain road. When they reached Hudaybiyyah his camel al-Qaswa knelt and would not rise. The Companions said she was stubborn. He said: "She is not stubborn; that is not her nature. She was stopped by the One who stopped the elephant. By Allah, whatever terms they ask me today that honour the sanctities of Allah, I will accept." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Quraysh sent several envoys. ‘Urwah ibn Mas’ud, an experienced man, returned amazed: "O people, by Allah, I have been to Chosroes and Caesar and the Negus, and I have never seen a king whose companions revere him like Muhammad’s companions revere Muhammad. If he spits, it falls in someone’s hand and he rubs it on his face and body. If he orders them, they rush to do it. If he performs ablution, they nearly fight over his water. They lower their voices in front of him and do not look him in the eye out of reverence." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The Prophet ﷺ sent ‘Uthman to Makkah, as he had kin to protect him. News spread that ‘Uthman had been killed. The Prophet ﷺ called the Muslims to pledge under a tree to fight to the death, and all except one man did so: "Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged to you under the tree." (48:18) It later turned out that ‘Uthman was safe.

Suhayl ibn ‘Amr arrived for Quraysh. The terms: a ten-year truce; the Muslims turn back this year and may return next year for three days; any Makkan who joins Muhammad without his guardian’s permission must be returned, but any Muslim who goes to Quraysh need not; and any tribe may ally with either side. When the Prophet ﷺ dictated "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," Suhayl objected: "We do not know this. Write, In Your name, O Allah." And when it said "Muhammad, Messenger of Allah," he said: "If we knew you were the Messenger of Allah, we would not have fought you. Write Muhammad ibn ‘Abdullah." The Prophet ﷺ agreed to both. When ‘Ali refused to erase the words "Messenger of Allah," the Prophet ﷺ asked where they were and erased them himself (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

The Muslims were deeply upset, and ‘Umar asked: "Are we not on the truth and they on falsehood? Why should we accept humiliation in our religion?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the Messenger of Allah; I will not disobey Him, and He will help me." ‘Umar then went to Abu Bakr with the same questions, and got the same answer, and later said he gave charity and fasted and freed slaves to atone for his words that day (Sahih al-Bukhari).

He told the Companions to sacrifice and shave their heads. None moved, three times. He went to his wife Umm Salamah, upset. She said: "O Prophet of Allah, do you want this? Go out, do not say a word to anyone until you have slaughtered your animal and called your barber." He did, and they all rose, sacrificing and shaving until they nearly crushed each other (Sahih al-Bukhari).

On the way back, Surah al-Fath was revealed: "Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest" (48:1). He told the Companions that a surah had been revealed to him that night that was dearer to him than everything the sun rises upon (Sahih al-Bukhari). The truce allowed the Arabs to meet Muslims in peace; many saw their character and converted. Khalid ibn al-Walid and ‘Amr ibn al-‘As accepted Islam in the following months.

Abu Basir, who had escaped Quraysh and had to be returned under the treaty, killed one of his guards on the way and settled at the coast, where others who fled joined him, and began intercepting Quraysh trade caravans. Quraysh themselves asked the Prophet ﷺ to take them in and drop the clause (Sahih al-Bukhari). Within two years, the treaty was broken by Quraysh’s allies, which led to the conquest of Makkah.

facts: A silver ring engraved "Muhammad Rasul Allah"
Heraclius, Khosrow, the Negus, the Muqawqis and others
The campaign of Khaybar, Muharram 7 AH

t: When it was suggested that rulers only read sealed letters, the Prophet ﷺ had a silver ring made, engraved with three lines: "Muhammad / Rasul / Allah" (Sahih al-Bukhari). He sent envoys to Heraclius, the Byzantine emperor; Khosrow Parviz of Persia; the Negus of Abyssinia; the Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt; and the leaders of several Arab kingdoms, inviting them to Islam.

The letter to Heraclius began: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, the servant of Allah and His Messenger, to Heraclius, ruler of the Byzantines. Peace be upon whoever follows the guidance. I invite you to the call of Islam. Accept Islam and you will be safe, and Allah will give you your reward twice. If you turn away, then upon you is the sin of the peasants." and the verse "Say, O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah." (3:64)

Heraclius happened to be in Jerusalem, and asked whether any Arabs from the prophet’s people were nearby. Abu Sufyan, in Syria on a trading trip and still an enemy, was brought in. Heraclius asked him questions through an interpreter: What is his family like? Did any of his family claim prophethood before? Did he have a king among his ancestors? Do the nobles follow him or the weak? Do his followers increase or decrease? Does anyone leave in anger? Has he ever betrayed? Have you ever accused him of lying before he claimed this? What does he command? Abu Sufyan answered honestly, although he later said he would have lied if he had not been ashamed of being called a liar.

Heraclius replied: "I asked about his lineage, and you said he is of noble lineage, and that is how prophets are sent. I asked if he lied before, and you said no; he would not lie about people and then lie about Allah. If what you say is true, he will rule the ground beneath my feet. I knew he would appear, but I did not think he would be from among you. If I could reach him, I would wash his feet." The court erupted and he had them thrown out. Heraclius did not convert, but he honoured the Prophet’s ﷺ letter. (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Khosrow tore up the letter in rage; when the Prophet ﷺ heard, he said: "May Allah tear his kingdom to pieces." (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Sira reports that the Negus answered respectfully and accepted Islam, and that the Muqawqis replied politely, sending gifts, among them Maryam al-Qibtiyyah, who bore the Prophet’s ﷺ son Ibrahim, and the white mule Duldul.

In Muharram 7 AH the Muslims marched on Khaybar, a fortified oasis of Jewish clans some 150 km north of Madinah, from which the exiled leaders of Banu al-Nadir had helped organise the coalition against Madinah. Only those who had been at Hudaybiyyah were permitted to go (48:15, 48:18–20). After several of its forts fell over a number of weeks, the Prophet ﷺ said he would give the banner the next day to a man whom Allah and His Messenger love, and it was given to ‘Ali (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

The people were allowed to remain and farm the land in return for half of the harvest. One of the women of Khaybar, Zaynab bint al-Harith, served the Prophet ﷺ a roasted, poisoned sheep. He spat out the first bite, and one Companion, Bishr ibn al-Bara’, who ate it, died (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sunan Abi Dawud). Ja’far and the emigrants of Abyssinia arrived back around the time Khaybar ended, and the Prophet ﷺ kissed Ja’far between the eyes and said he did not know which was the cause of greater joy: Khaybar’s conquest or Ja’far’s arrival (as reported in the Sira).

facts: Mu’tah, east of the Jordan, in the Byzantine sphere
A far larger force of Byzantines and allied Arab tribes
Zayd ibn Harithah, Ja’far ibn Abi Talib, ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah

t: The Prophet ﷺ had sent an envoy, al-Harith ibn ‘Umayr al-Azdi, with a letter to the ruler of Busra. Shurahbil ibn ‘Amr al-Ghassani, a Byzantine-allied chieftain, killed him, which was a grave breach of the rule that messengers are not harmed. The Prophet ﷺ sent three thousand men north to hold the killers to account.

He appointed three commanders in order: "If Zayd is killed, Ja’far takes command; if Ja’far is killed, ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah." (Sahih al-Bukhari). Zayd was his freed servant and adopted son; Ja’far, his cousin, who had led the migrants to Abyssinia; ‘Abdullah, a poet of the Ansar. Their appointment together shows he judged people by capacity, not tribe.

At Mu’tah the Muslims found a force of Byzantine troops and Arab allies many times larger than theirs. After two nights of debate, ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah reminded them: "By Allah, what you hate is the very thing you came out for: martyrdom. We do not fight people by number, strength or large numbers but by this religion Allah has honoured us with. Go, for it is one of two excellent things: victory or martyrdom."

Zayd carried the banner and fought until he was killed. Ja’far took it; when his right hand was cut off, he held it in his left, and when that was cut off, he clasped the banner to his chest until he was killed. ‘Abdullah took it, hesitated for a moment, then recited verses to himself and fought on until he fell. ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar later found Ja’far among the dead and counted over ninety wounds from spears and arrows in his body (Sahih al-Bukhari).

The Muslims chose Khalid ibn al-Walid, who had accepted Islam only a few months before. He held the army together through the day. The next morning he rearranged the ranks so that the enemy, seeing new faces and standards, believed reinforcements had arrived. After skirmishing, he withdrew in good order. Khalid said nine swords broke in his hand that day (Sahih al-Bukhari).

In Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ stood on the pulpit and told the people before any messenger arrived: "Zayd took the banner and was martyred; then Ja’far took it and was martyred; then Ibn Rawahah took it and was martyred," and his eyes were flowing with tears. "Then the banner was taken by a sword of the swords of Allah (Khalid), until Allah gave them victory." (Sahih al-Bukhari). He went to Ja’far’s family to comfort them, and told them to prepare food for them, since they were occupied with their loss (Sunan Abi Dawud).

facts: Quraysh’s allies broke the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah by attacking Khuza’ah

t: Two years into the Hudaybiyyah truce, Banu Bakr, allies of Quraysh, attacked Khuza’ah, allies of the Prophet ﷺ, and Quraysh helped them with weapons. Khuza’ah appealed to Madinah. Quraysh realised their mistake and sent Abu Sufyan to renew the treaty, but he failed. The Prophet ﷺ began to prepare in secrecy.

Hatib ibn Abi Balta’ah, a veteran of Badr with family left in Makkah, sent a woman with a letter warning Quraysh. The Prophet ﷺ learned by revelation, sent ‘Ali and al-Zubayr to intercept her, and read the letter. When ‘Umar asked to execute Hatib, the Prophet ﷺ asked him why he did it. Hatib said he had no tribal protection for his family and meant no betrayal. The Prophet ﷺ accepted his explanation and reminded ‘Umar that Hatib had fought at Badr. Surah al-Mumtahanah 60:1 was revealed (Sahih al-Bukhari).

About ten thousand set out. At Marr al-Zahran, a day from Makkah, they camped and lit ten thousand fires. Abu Sufyan, Hakim ibn Hizam and Budayl ibn Warqa’ went out to see and were stunned. Al-‘Abbas brought Abu Sufyan to the Prophet ﷺ, and he accepted Islam. Al-‘Abbas asked the Prophet ﷺ to give him some honour, and he declared: "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe, whoever shuts his door is safe, and whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe." (Sahih Muslim)

The Prophet ﷺ entered riding his camel, his head so low in humility that his beard almost touched the saddle, reciting Surah al-Fath (Sahih al-Bukhari). He had told the commanders to avoid fighting unless attacked. There was a small clash at one entrance, where some Makkans fought Khalid’s column, and a few men were killed.

He went to the Kaaba, circled it, and with a stick struck the idols around it, one after another, reciting: "The truth has come, and falsehood has departed. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to depart." (17:81) The idols fell. He entered the Kaaba, had the pictures inside removed and prayed (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). He took the key from ‘Uthman ibn Talhah, then handed it back to him and his family to keep, in line with the verse "Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due." (4:58) (as reported in the Sira).

s.h: The people who had fought him
t: He stood at the door of the Kaaba and addressed Quraysh, who had been his enemies for twenty years, who had tortured the Muslims, driven them from their homes and fought them at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. The Sira reports that he asked: "O Quraysh, what do you think I will do with you?" They said, "Good. You are a noble brother, son of a noble brother." He said: "Go, for you are free." A very small number of people, whose crimes were exceptional, were excluded from the general amnesty, and some of them, like ‘Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, were pardoned afterwards when they came to seek forgiveness. Wahshi, who killed Hamzah, also accepted Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ asked only that he stay out of his sight.

Then he told the Muslims at the gathering: "Allah made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth; it is sacred by Allah’s sanctity until the Day of Resurrection." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Bilal climbed to the roof of the Kaaba and gave the adhan. He remained in Makkah for about nineteen days, shortening his prayers (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Surah al-Nasr was revealed: "When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes, then exalt [Allah] with praise of your Lord and ask forgiveness of Him. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance." ‘A’ishah said that after it was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said in his bowing and prostration very often: "Glory be to You, our Lord, and praise; O Allah, forgive me." (Sahih al-Bukhari). Ibn ‘Abbas and ‘Umar understood it as a sign that his work was nearly complete.

facts: Hawazin and Thaqif, led by Malik ibn ‘Awf
The valley of Hunayn, between Makkah and Ta’if

t: Hawazin and Thaqif gathered a large force and, according to the Sira, brought along their families and animals so that their men would not flee. They hid in the narrow valley of Hunayn.
