"O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters [requiring] determination." (31:17)

"And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful. And be moderate in your pace and lower your voice; indeed, the most disagreeable of sounds is the voice of donkeys." (31:18–19)

The advice moves from belief to family, to accountability, to worship, to society and finally to manners. A complete character is built in nine sentences. Notably, nothing in it asks the son for worldly success: it is about who he is.

facts: The people of Musa, who "oppressed them" (28:76)
Treasures whose keys alone were a burden to a strong band
"I was only given it because of knowledge I have"
The earth swallowed him and his home

t: His own people warned him: "Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not like the exultant. But seek, through that which Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and [yet], do not forget your share of the world. And do good as Allah has done good to you. And desire not corruption in the land. Indeed, Allah does not like corrupters." (28:76–77) It is a complete economic ethic: wealth is allowed, even with a share in this world, but it must be used for the next, and not spent on corruption.

He said: "I was only given it because of knowledge I have." (28:78) Allah answered: "Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him of generations those who were greater than him in power and greater in accumulation?" Qarun went out among his people in his adornment. Those who desired worldly life said: "Oh, would that we had the like of what was given to Qarun. Indeed, he is one of great fortune." But those who had been given knowledge said: "Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for he who believes and does righteousness. And none are granted it except the steadfast." (28:79–80)

"So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. And there was for him no company to aid him other than Allah, nor was he of those who [could] defend themselves. And those who had wished for his position the previous day began to say: Oh, how Allah extends provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it]! If it had not been that Allah conferred favour on us, He would have caused it to swallow us. Oh, how the disbelievers do not succeed!" (28:81–82)

The Qur’an concludes with a general principle: "That home of the Hereafter We assign to those who do not desire exaltedness upon the earth or corruption. And the [best] outcome is for the righteous." (28:83)

facts: "Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the companions of the garden"
To harvest at dawn, leaving nothing for the poor
"Glory to our Lord; indeed, we were wrongdoers"

t: The story was told to Quraysh as a warning, since Allah had given them prosperity as a test: "Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the companions of the garden, when they swore to harvest it in the early morning, and were not making exception." (68:17–18) "Making exception" means saying "if Allah wills." They were so sure of their plan that they did not acknowledge Allah’s will.

"So there came upon it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep, and it became as though it had been reaped." (68:19–20) In the morning they called each other: "Go early to your crop if you would harvest." They set out, speaking in whispers: "No poor person will enter it today upon you." And they went early, determined, able. But when they saw it, they said: "Indeed, we are lost." Then they said: "Rather, we have been deprived." (68:21–27)

Then "the most moderate of them said: Did I not say to you, Why do you not exalt [Allah]?" They said: "Exalted is our Lord! Indeed, we were wrongdoers." They turned to blaming one another. "They said: O woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors. Perhaps our Lord will substitute for us one better than it. Indeed, we are toward our Lord desirous." (68:28–32) The Qur’an concludes: "Such is the punishment [of this world]. And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew." (68:33)

Two sins: the greed that denies the poor a share of what Allah gave, and the arrogance of planning without mention of His will. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever says, insha’allah, when he swears, will not be in breach." Allah directed in Surah al-Kahf: "And never say of anything, Indeed, I will do that tomorrow, except [with the addition], If Allah wills." (18:23–24)

facts: The Year of the Elephant, c. 570 CE, the year the Prophet ﷺ was born
Abraha, governor of Yemen under the Kingdom of Aksum
Birds with stones of baked clay (105:3–4)

t: Abraha built a magnificent cathedral in Sana’a, intending to divert the Arab pilgrimage from Makkah. The Sira tells that an Arab man defiled it in anger. Abraha swore to destroy the Kaaba and marched north with a large army and several elephants, among them a big one named Mahmud. Several Arab tribes tried to resist and were defeated.

At the outskirts of Makkah, Abraha’s men seized two hundred camels belonging to ‘Abd al-Muttalib, the leader of Quraysh. He went to speak to Abraha, who was impressed by his appearance and asked what he wanted. He said: "I want my two hundred camels." Abraha said: "I was impressed by you when I saw you, and now I regret it. You speak to me about two hundred camels and say nothing about the House, which is your religion and your fathers’ religion, which I have come to destroy?" ‘Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the owner of the camels, and the House has an Owner who will protect it." The Quraysh withdrew into the hills and prayed at the Kaaba.

When Abraha’s army was ordered to advance, the elephant knelt, and would not go toward the Kaaba, though it went when turned in other directions (as the Sira tells). Then, "He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and made them like eaten straw." (105:3–5) The Sira adds that Abraha was struck by a disease that made his body fall apart, and that he died soon after reaching Yemen.

Surah al-Fil begins: "Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?" The Prophet ﷺ’s generation could remember it. The Arabs counted time from this year, and the story shows how Allah protected the House before it had a prophet to defend it.

facts: A king, his sorcerer, a boy, a monk
"Be patient, mother, for you are on the truth"

s.h: The sorcerer, the boy and the monk
t: Suhayb reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: There was a king, and he had a sorcerer. When the sorcerer grew old, he asked the king to send him a boy to teach. The boy, on his way, would pass a monk, and sit and listen to him, and he liked what he heard. When he went to the sorcerer, he was beaten for being late, and when he went home, he was beaten for being late. He complained to the monk, who said: "When you fear the sorcerer, say, The people of my house held me up; and when you fear your family, say, The sorcerer held me up."

One day a huge animal blocked the road. The boy said: "Today I will know whether the sorcerer or the monk is better." He took a stone and said, "O Allah, if the way of the monk is more beloved to You than that of the sorcerer, kill this animal so that people may pass," and he threw it and killed it. The people passed. He told the monk, who said: "My son, today you are better than me; you have reached what I see. You will be tested; if you are, do not tell on me."

The boy healed the blind and the lepers, and cured people of illnesses. A blind courtier of the king, hearing of him, brought a large gift and asked to be healed. The boy said: "I do not heal anyone. Allah heals. If you believe in Allah, I will pray and He will heal you." The courtier believed and was healed. Then he sat before the king as he used to, and the king asked: "Who restored your sight?" "My Lord." "Do you have a lord other than me?" "My Lord and your Lord is Allah." The king tortured him until he told of the boy, then tortured the boy until he told of the monk. The king ordered the monk and the courtier to renounce their religion. They refused, and he had them sawn in two.

The king sent men to take the boy up a mountain and throw him from the top if he did not leave his faith. The boy prayed: "O Allah, save me from them as You wish," and the mountain shook, and they fell, and the boy walked back to the king. Then a boat sent to drown him in the middle of the sea. He prayed the same, and it capsized, and all drowned; he walked back to the king. The boy said: "You will not be able to kill me until you do as I command." The king asked: "What?" He said: "Gather the people in a single place, tie me to a trunk, take an arrow from my quiver and say, In the name of Allah, the Lord of the boy; then shoot me. If you do that, you will be able to kill me."

The king did, and placed the arrow in his bow, saying "In the name of Allah, the Lord of the boy." The arrow hit the boy’s temple. The boy put his hand to the wound and died. The people cried out: "We believe in the Lord of the boy!" three times.

The king’s courtiers said: "Do you see what you feared? By Allah, what you feared has come: the people have believed." So the king commanded for trenches to be dug at the entrances of the roads, and fires lit in them. He said: "Whoever does not return from his religion, throw him in it." They did, until a woman came with her baby, and she hesitated to fall in. The baby said: "O mother, be patient, for you are on the truth." (Sahih Muslim)

Surah al-Buruj says: "Destroyed were the companions of the trench, [containing] the fire full of fuel, when they were sitting near it and they, to what they were doing against the believers, were witnesses. And they resented them not except because they believed in Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy." (85:4–8) Then it promises: "Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the great success." (85:11)

facts: A believing man of Fir’awn’s household who hid his faith
"I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of [His] servants"
Why the surah is called Ghafir

t: When Fir’awn said, "Let me kill Musa and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption in the land," (40:26) a believer from among his own people, "who concealed his faith," spoke up: "Do you kill a man [merely] because he says, My Lord is Allah, while he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he should be lying, then upon him is [the consequence of] his lie; but if he should be truthful, there will strike you some of what he promises you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar." (40:28)

He used reason and he used history. First: "O my people, you have today [high] position in the land, [but] who would aid us against the punishment of Allah if it came to us?" Fir’awn answered: "I do not show you except what I see, and I do not guide you except to the way of right conduct." The man warned: "O my people, indeed I fear for you [a fate] like the day of the companions [of earlier prophets], like the custom of the people of Nuh and ‘Ad and Thamud and those after them." (40:29–31) Then of the Day of Resurrection, and Yusuf, who had come before with clear proofs, and they did not believe him until he died. (40:32–34)

He spoke to their conscience: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct. O my people, this worldly life is only [temporary] enjoyment, and indeed, the Hereafter is the home of [permanent] settlement." (40:38–39) And finally: "You will remember what I [now] say to you, and I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of [His] servants." (40:44)

"So Allah protected him from the evils which they plotted, and there enveloped the people of Fir’awn the worst of punishment." (40:45) The Qur’an describes how they are brought before the Fire morning and evening in their graves, and that on the Day when the Hour is established, "Make the people of Fir’awn enter the severest punishment." (40:46) The believer is nameless in the Qur’an. Commentators give names, but they are not part of the revelation. What we have of him is a voice: courageous, rational, kind.

facts: A town the Qur’an does not name; commentators differ
Two, then a third to support them
A man from the farthest part of the city
Said on his entry to Paradise

t: "And present to them an example: [the story of] the people of the town, when the messengers came to it. When We sent to them two but they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, and they said, Indeed, we are messengers to you." The people answered: "You are only human beings like ourselves, and the Most Merciful has not sent down anything. You are only telling lies." The messengers said: "Our Lord knows that we are messengers to you, and we are only responsible for clear notification." They said: "Indeed, we consider you a bad omen. If you do not cease, we will surely stone you, and there will surely touch you from us a painful punishment." They said: "Your omen is with yourselves. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a transgressing people." (36:13–19)

"And there came from the farthest end of the city a man, running. He said: O my people, follow the messengers. Follow those who do not ask you for payment, and they are [rightly] guided. And why should I not worship He who created me and to whom you will be returned? Should I take other than Him as gods when, if the Most Merciful intends for me some adversity, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they save me? Indeed, I would then be in manifest error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me." (36:20–25)

The Qur’an does not describe how they killed him, only that "It was said, Enter Paradise." He said: "If only my people could know of how my Lord has forgiven me and placed me among the honoured." (36:26–27) Commentators note that even after what they did to him, his first thought was to wish them well.

Allah did not send an army from the heaven against them: "There was not but one shout, and immediately they were extinguished." (36:29) And: "How regrettable for the servants. There did not come to them any messenger except that they used to ridicule him." (36:30) The story ends in a few lines, because the lesson was in the man’s words and his unexpected generosity of heart.

facts: The elders of Bani Isra’il, from their prophet
A river: whoever drinks is not with me

t: The elders of Bani Isra’il, remembering their losses, asked their prophet: "Send to us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah." The prophet said: "Might it be that if fighting was prescribed for you, you would not fight?" They said: "And why should we not fight in the cause of Allah when we have been driven out from our homes and from our children?" But when fighting was written upon them, they turned away, except for a few (2:246).

Their prophet said: "Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as a king." They said: "How can he have kingship over us while we are more worthy of kingship than he and he has not been given any measure of wealth?" He said: "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature." The sign of his kingship was that the Ark would come to them, "in which is tranquillity from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun had left, carried by the angels" (2:247–248).

When Talut went out with the soldiers he said: "Indeed, Allah will be testing you with a river. So whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is indeed of me, except one who takes [from it] in the hand." They drank from it, except a few. When he and those who believed crossed it, they said: "There is no power for us today against Jalut and his soldiers." But those who were certain that they would meet Allah said: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast." (2:249)

They prayed as they met the enemy: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience and plant firmly our feet and give us victory over the disbelieving people." (2:250) They defeated them by Allah’s permission, and Dawud killed Jalut. Allah gave him kingship and wisdom (2:251).

The story is about three tests: a test of obedience to a leader who is not rich, a test of discipline at the river, and a test of faith before an overwhelming force. And the Qur’an adds a principle for history: "If Allah had not checked the people, some by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted." (2:251)

facts: One rich and arrogant, one poor and a believer
"I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in numbers"
"Why did you not say, Ma sha’ Allah, la quwwata illa billah?"
The gardens ruined; he wrung his hands

t: "And present to them an example of two men: to one of them We granted two gardens of grapevines and bordered them with palm trees and placed between them [fields of] crops. Each of the two gardens produced its fruit and did not fall short of it in anything. And We caused to burst forth within them a river." (18:32–33) He said to his companion as they talked: "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in manpower." (18:34)

He entered his garden, "while he was unjust to himself," and said: "I do not think that this will perish, ever. And I do not think the Hour will occur. And even if I should be brought back to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return." (18:35–36) His companion told him: "Have you disbelieved in He who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then proportioned you [as] a man? But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate with my Lord anyone." (18:37–38)

"And why did you, when you entered your garden, not say, What Allah willed [has occurred]; there is no power except in Allah? Although you see me less than you in wealth and children, it may be that my Lord will give me [something] better than your garden and will send upon it a calamity from the sky, and it will become a smooth, dusty ground." (18:39–40)

"And his fruits were encompassed [by ruin], and he began to turn his hands about [in dismay] over what he had spent on it, while it was bare on its trellises, and said: Oh, I wish that I had not associated with my Lord anyone." (18:42) There was no company to help him other than Allah. "There the authority is [completely] for Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome." (18:43–44)

The practical lesson became a saying of the Muslims: when you see something you like, say "Ma sha’ Allah, la quwwata illa billah." The Prophet ﷺ taught that "la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah" is a treasure from the treasures of Paradise (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid ibn Asad of Quraysh
About 595 CE; she was the Prophet’s first wife
Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, al-Qasim and ‘Abdullah
In the 10th year of prophethood, about three years before the Hijrah
"The best of the women of her time" (Sahih al-Bukhari)

s.h: A woman of business and character
t: Khadijah was known in Makkah as al-Tahirah, the pure. She had been widowed twice and ran a large trading business, hiring men to carry her goods. When she heard of the honesty of Muhammad ibn ‘Abdullah, she asked him to trade for her, and offered him more than she normally paid. On his return, her servant Maysarah told her what he had observed: his integrity, his courtesy and the way he dealt with people. She then proposed marriage through a friend. It was a marriage in which she, a woman of status, took the initiative, and it lasted twenty-five years.

After the first revelation, the Prophet ﷺ came home trembling. Her response, preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari, was not panic but reasoning from his character: "By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You maintain family ties, bear the burdens of the weak, give to those who have nothing, honour guests and help in cases of hardship." She believed before anyone else, and took him to Waraqah. For the next ten years, she shared in the opposition, the boycott in the valley of Abu Talib and the loss of her wealth, which she placed at his disposal.

‘A’ishah, who married him after Khadijah’s death, said: "I was never jealous of any of the wives of the Prophet as I was of Khadijah, though I never saw her, because of how much he mentioned her. Whenever he slaughtered a sheep he would say: Send some to the friends of Khadijah." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Abu Hurayrah narrates that Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, here is Khadijah, with a vessel containing food and drink. When she comes, convey to her the greetings of her Lord, and my greetings, and give her glad tidings of a house in Paradise of pearl, in which is no noise and no toil." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Quhafah, of the clan of Taym
Al-Siddiq (the one who affirms the truth)
11–13 AH (632–634 CE), about two years and three months
In the cave of Thawr and at every major event

t: He was a wealthy, trusted and well-liked merchant of Makkah. When the Prophet ﷺ told him of the revelation, he accepted at once. The Prophet ﷺ said later: "I did not invite anyone to Islam except that he hesitated, was reluctant and thought, except Abu Bakr; he did not hesitate when I mentioned it to him." (as reported in the Sira). Through him, several of the great Companions accepted Islam, and he spent his wealth to free persecuted slaves: Bilal, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah and others. A verse was revealed praising one "who gave and feared Allah and believed in the best" (92:5–7), which commentators connect to him.

s.h: In the cave and on the journey
t: In the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ chose Abu Bakr as his only companion on the road. In the cave of Thawr, he was afraid for the Prophet ﷺ and not for himself. The Qur’an names him by a phrase: "the second of two" (9:40). The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no one who has been more generous to me in his company and his property than Abu Bakr. Had I taken a khalil other than my Lord, I would have taken Abu Bakr." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

‘Umar ibn al-Khattab reports that the Prophet ﷺ commanded charity at the time of Tabuk, and ‘Umar thought: "Today I will surpass Abu Bakr." He brought half his wealth. The Prophet ﷺ asked what he had left for his family; he said, "The same amount." Then Abu Bakr brought all he had. The Prophet ﷺ asked what he left for his family. He said: "Allah and His Messenger." ‘Umar said: "I will never compete with you in anything." (Sunan Abi Dawud and al-Tirmidhi)

At the Prophet’s ﷺ death, he steadied the people with the verse "Muhammad is not but a messenger" (3:144), and was chosen as the first caliph at the Saqifah of Banu Sa’idah. In his short rule he dispatched the army of Usamah that the Prophet ﷺ had prepared, put down the tribes that refused zakah and those who claimed prophethood, and ordered the collection of the Qur’an into a single volume after many reciters were killed at the Battle of Yamamah (Sahih al-Bukhari, Zayd ibn Thabit). In his first speech, he said: "Obey me as long as I obey Allah and His Messenger. If I disobey, you owe me no obedience."

facts: ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, of the clan of ‘Adi
Al-Faruq (the one who distinguishes truth from falsehood)
13–23 AH (634–644 CE), about ten and a half years
Dhul-Hijjah, 23 AH, after being stabbed while leading Fajr prayer

t: The Sira tells of ‘Umar setting out with his sword to find the Prophet ﷺ. A man on the road, Nu’aym ibn ‘Abdullah, told him to put his own house in order, because his sister Fatimah and her husband Sa’id had accepted Islam. He went there and heard recitation, and struck his brother-in-law and hit his sister so that she bled. She said: "Do what you will, we have become Muslim." Seeing the blood, he felt ashamed and asked to see what they were reading. She told him to wash first. He read the opening of Surah Ta-Ha: "We have not sent down to you the Qur’an that you be distressed, but only as a reminder for those who fear [Allah]" and said: "How beautiful and noble is this speech." He went to the house of al-Arqam and declared his Islam. (As reported in the Sira.)
‘Abdullah ibn Mas’ud said: "We have been mighty since ‘Umar became Muslim." (Sahih al-Bukhari) Before him, the Muslims prayed secretly; after, they prayed at the Kaaba.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "If there were a prophet after me, he would be ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi). He also said: "Satan does not meet ‘Umar on a path but he takes another path." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Many verses were revealed in agreement with his view, including the Station of Ibrahim, the hijab and the prisoners of Badr. Yet he was also gently corrected: at Hudaybiyyah he questioned the terms of the treaty, and when the Prophet ﷺ died he at first could not bring himself to believe it.

During his time as caliph, Muslim rule reached Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia. He established the Hijri calendar, the diwan (a register that paid stipends from the treasury), and courts. His justice is remembered in stories: he patrolled Madinah at night; hearing a mother pretend to cook stones to quiet her hungry children, he carried a sack of flour on his own back to her house (as reported by early historians). He is reported to have said: "If a mule were to stumble in Iraq, I fear that Allah would ask me why I did not pave the road for it." He was stabbed by Abu Lu’lu’ah, a Persian slave, while leading the Fajr prayer, and he died three days later, asking to be buried beside the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (Sahih al-Bukhari).

facts: Makkah, to an Abyssinian mother (Hamamah); a slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf
The Prophet ﷺ heard his footsteps in Paradise (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

t: Bilal believed early. His master Umayyah ibn Khalaf took him out in the heat of the day, laid him on the burning sand, placed a huge rock on his chest and said: "You will stay here until you die or deny Muhammad and worship al-Lat and al-‘Uzza." He kept repeating: "Ahad, ahad" (One, One). Abu Bakr passed, and said to Umayyah: "Do you not fear Allah for this poor man? How long?" Umayyah said: "You corrupted him; save him." Abu Bakr said he would, and bought him with a stronger slave and freed him (as reported in the Sira). Years later at Badr, Bilal saw Umayyah among the captives and cried out, and the Muslims killed him.

In Madinah, when the adhan was introduced, the Prophet ﷺ told ‘Abdullah ibn Zayd to teach it to Bilal, "for he has a more beautiful voice than you" (Sunan Abi Dawud). He called the Muslims to prayer for the rest of the Prophet’s life. On the day Makkah was conquered, he climbed on the Kaaba and gave the adhan. A once-enslaved Abyssinian man gave the call to prayer on the holiest building in Islam, a point not lost on the Makkans who had tortured him.

The Prophet ﷺ said to Bilal at Fajr: "O Bilal, tell me of the best deed you have done in Islam, for I heard the sound of your footsteps in front of me in Paradise." Bilal said: "I have not done anything better, except that whenever I perform wudu at any time of day or night, I pray with that purity what Allah wills me to pray." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

After the Prophet ﷺ died, Bilal found it too painful to call the adhan in Madinah and went to Syria. The Sira tells that once he came back, and the Prophet’s ﷺ grandsons al-Hasan and al-Husayn asked him to give the adhan once more, and when he did, Madinah wept as it had when the Prophet ﷺ was alive.

facts: ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet’s cousin

s.h: A child in the Prophet’s house
t: When Makkah suffered a famine, the Prophet ﷺ took ‘Ali, then a small boy, into his own household to relieve Abu Talib, who had many children. He grew up beside the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam at about ten. He was given the most dangerous job on the night of the Hijrah, to lie in the Prophet’s ﷺ bed, covered in his cloak, while the men of Quraysh watched. Then he stayed behind for three days to return the trusts people had left with the Prophet ﷺ, and followed on foot to Madinah.

At Khaybar the Muslims were struggling to take the fort. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man through whom Allah will grant victory, who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love." The Companions spent the night wondering who it would be. In the morning, he asked: "Where is ‘Ali?" They said he had a sore eye. The Prophet ﷺ applied his saliva to it and ‘Ali was healed as if he had never had pain. He gave him the banner, and told him to invite them to Islam before fighting, saying: "By Allah, if Allah guides one man through you, it is better for you than red camels." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

He was among the foremost jurists and judges of the Companions; It is reported that ‘Umar used to say, "May Allah not let me live in a predicament where ‘Ali is not present to solve it." He lived simply, even when he was caliph. As the fourth caliph he ruled in the most difficult time, when the community was divided after the killing of ‘Uthman. He was killed by Ibn Muljam, a Kharijite, while going to the Fajr prayer in Kufah, in Ramadan 40 AH.
The Prophet ﷺ said to him on the way to Tabuk: "Are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me?" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: Dhu al-Nurayn (possessor of two lights), for marrying two daughters of the Prophet
Generosity, modesty, and the standard copy of the Qur’an
In his house in Madinah, in 35 AH

t: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Should I not be shy of a man of whom the angels are shy?" (Sahih Muslim). ‘Uthman had given most of his time and wealth to Islam: he emigrated twice, to Abyssinia and Madinah. When the Muslims in Madinah lacked good water, the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever bought the well of Rumah would have Paradise. ‘Uthman bought it and made it available to everyone (Sunan al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa’i). At Tabuk he provided hundreds of camels with saddles and blankets and a thousand dinars, which he poured into the Prophet’s ﷺ lap, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "Nothing ‘Uthman does after today will harm him." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi)

During the conquest of Armenia and Azerbaijan, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman saw Muslims from different regions disputing over recitation. He told ‘Uthman: "Save this nation before they differ about the Book as the Jews and Christians did." ‘Uthman asked Hafsah for the volume that had been compiled in Abu Bakr’s time, and appointed Zayd ibn Thabit, ‘Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa’id ibn al-‘As and ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith to copy it, in the dialect of Quraysh in case of disagreement. Copies were sent to the major cities, and the other copies were burnt (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Qur’an read today follows that standard text, the same in every land.

In his last years, discontent grew among some of the provinces, partly over appointments of his relatives. Rebels came to Madinah and besieged his house for weeks. He had the strength and the Companions’ offer to fight, but he refused to shed Muslim blood to defend himself, saying that the Prophet ﷺ had told him that Allah may clothe him in a garment and people would want him to remove it, and not to remove it (Sunan al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah). He was killed while reading the Qur’an. His death opened a period of civil strife.

facts: About 2,210 hadith (the number counted by the hadith scholars)
Among them ‘Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, al-Qasim and Masruq
Ramadan, 58 AH (678 CE), buried in al-Baqi’
In her room, in her arms

t: Abu Musa al-Ash’ari said: "Whenever we, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, had difficulty over a matter and asked ‘A’ishah, we found she had knowledge of it." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi). She explained verses, issued legal verdicts and corrected other Companions where she thought they had misunderstood. Her student ‘Urwah said he had never seen anyone more knowledgeable in fiqh, medicine or poetry. Many details of the Prophet’s ﷺ private life and worship are known only because she narrated them.

She told how he used to be "in the service of his family", helping with household chores, mending his shoes and sewing his clothes, and "when the call to prayer came he would go out" (Sahih al-Bukhari). When asked whom he loved most, he said "‘A’ishah." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). They raced each other once, and she won; later, when she was heavier, he won, and said, "This is for that." (Sunan Abi Dawud).

On the way back from the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, ‘A’ishah was left behind when her camel was loaded without her, and was brought back by Safwan ibn al-Mu’attal. The hypocrites, led by ‘Abdullah ibn Ubayy, spread a rumour. For a month the Prophet ﷺ received no revelation about it, and she wept constantly. When he came to her and said she should repent if she had sinned, she said she would say what Yusuf’s father said: "So patience is most fitting." Then revelation came: ten verses of Surah al-Nur (24:11–20) declared her innocence. She said: "I did not think that Allah would send down a revelation that would be recited about me." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: In 621 CE, as the first envoy of Islam

t: He grew up in a rich home, with fine perfume and costly clothes, and the Sira says that Makkah had no young man of his age who was better dressed. When he accepted Islam in secret, his mother, who adored him, found out, locked him up and withheld food and comfort. He escaped and emigrated to Abyssinia, and when he returned, he was thin and in worn clothes. The Prophet ﷺ saw him in a wrapped cloak with patches, and said to the Companions: "Look at him, whose heart Allah has illumined. I saw him with his parents who gave him the best food and drink; he left it for love of Allah and His Messenger." (as reported in the Sira)

After the first pledge of ‘Aqabah, the Prophet ﷺ sent him to Yathrib. Staying with As’ad ibn Zurarah, he taught the Qur’an, led the prayer and visited homes. By the following hajj, he had so many Muslims with him that seventy-five of them made the second pledge. He was gentle and clear, not argumentative. He was the one who turned the leaders Sa’d ibn Mu’adh and Usayd ibn Hudayr, and with them most of the clans of Aws, to Islam.

He carried the banner of the Muslims at Badr and again at Uhud. When the Muslim line broke, he held the banner high and fought for the Prophet ﷺ until he was killed, in the reports, by Ibn Qami’ah, who thought he had killed the Prophet ﷺ since Mus’ab resembled him. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: "We emigrated with the Messenger of Allah seeking Allah’s face, and Allah owed us our reward. Among us were those who died without eating any of their reward, such as Mus’ab ibn ‘Umayr, who was killed at Uhud and did not leave anything but a striped cloak. When we covered his head with it, his feet were uncovered, and when we covered his feet, his head was uncovered. The Prophet ﷺ told us to cover his head and put some idhkhir grass over his feet." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: About 615 CE, killed by Abu Jahl (as reported)

t: Yasir came from Yemen and settled in Makkah under the protection of Abu Hudhayfah of Banu Makhzum, who married him to his slave Sumayyah. Their son ‘Ammar was among the earliest Muslims. Because they were not of a powerful clan, they were exposed. Quraysh took them out to the burning plain of Makkah each day to force them to renounce Islam.

The Prophet ﷺ passed by them while they were being tortured and said: "Be patient, O family of Yasir, for your meeting place is Paradise." (as reported in the Sira and by al-Hakim). Yasir died under torture. The biographies say Sumayyah was killed by Abu Jahl, who speared her when she would not renounce her faith, which made her the first martyr of Islam. ‘Ammar, under duress, said words he did not mean, then came to the Prophet ﷺ in tears. He asked, "How do you find your heart?" ‘Ammar said, "Content with faith." The Prophet ﷺ said: "If they do it again, then say it again." (as reported by al-Bayhaqi, in connection with 16:106)

After Badr, the Prophet ﷺ told ‘Ammar: "Allah has judged your case against the killer of your mother." She is remembered as one of the great examples of steadfastness: a woman, enslaved, with no tribe to protect her, who stayed firm against one of the most powerful men in Makkah.

facts: Persia, in a Zoroastrian family (said to be from Isfahan or Ramhurmuz)
Persia → Syria → Mosul → Nisibis → Ammuriyah → Madinah

t: Salman told his own story to ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas, which is preserved in Musnad Ahmad. As a boy, he was devoted to the fire temple. Passing a church one day, he saw Christians praying, and found it better than his religion, so he asked where it came from and learned that it was in Syria. He ran away, travelled to a bishop, and served him. When the bishop died, he found out that he had been hoarding charity money and told the people. He moved to another teacher, and each in turn directed him to the next, until the last, dying at Ammuriyah, told him that a prophet would come in the land of Arabia, between two lava fields with palm trees, who accepted gifts but not charity, and had a seal of prophethood between his shoulders.

He travelled with a caravan of Arab traders who took him and sold him as a slave. He ended up in Madinah. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived, he brought food as charity; the Prophet ﷺ said to his companions to eat, but did not eat himself. The next day he brought a gift; the Prophet ﷺ ate it. Then he saw the seal between the shoulders, and kissed it and wept, and accepted Islam. The Prophet ﷺ helped him buy his freedom from his master, by planting three hundred palm trees and giving some gold the size of a hen’s egg.

At the Trench, he suggested digging a ditch around the vulnerable side, as Persian armies did. Both the Muhajirun and the Ansar said "Salman is one of us"; the Prophet ﷺ said: "Salman is from us, the people of the house." (reported by al-Hakim; the chain is weak, but the esteem in which the Companions held him is well attested). He took part in the conquest of Persia, and under ‘Umar was made governor of al-Mada’in, but kept to a wage of five thousand dirhams, which he gave away, living by weaving palm leaves. He is remembered for his advice that people should be moderate in worship.

facts: A shepherd for ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu’ayt
The great reciter, faqih of Kufah
Directly by the Prophet ﷺ: 70 surahs from his mouth
32 AH in Madinah, about 60 years old

t: He was a small, thin young man with slender legs. One day, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr, tired and thirsty, asked him for milk. He said he was entrusted with the sheep and could not. The Prophet ﷺ asked for a young ewe that had never been milked, and stroked its udder, and milk flowed. After they drank, the Prophet ﷺ told the udder to return to its place, and it did. Ibn Mas’ud said: "Teach me from this speech." The Prophet ﷺ stroked his head and said: "You are a learned boy." (Musnad Ahmad)

The Companions in Makkah were too afraid to recite the Qur’an in public. They said: "By Allah, Quraysh have never heard the Qur’an openly. Who will make them hear it?" Ibn Mas’ud said: "I will." They said they feared for him. He went to the Kaaba at midday, stood at the Station and began Surah al-Rahman. They hit him in the face, and he kept reciting as far as he could. His face was swollen when he returned. He said: "The enemies of Allah were never lighter in my eyes than today. If you wish I will do the same tomorrow." They said: "Enough." (as reported in the Sira)

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever loves to recite the Qur’an as fresh as it was revealed, let him recite according to the recitation of Ibn Umm ‘Abd (Ibn Mas’ud)." (Musnad Ahmad and Ibn Majah). One day he said to him: "Recite to me." Ibn Mas’ud said: "Shall I recite to you when it was revealed to you?" He said: "I like to hear it from others." He recited Surah al-Nisa’, and when he reached "How then if We bring from every nation a witness and We bring you against these as a witness?" (4:41), the Prophet ﷺ said: "Enough for now." Ibn Mas’ud looked and the Prophet’s ﷺ eyes were flowing with tears. (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: Al-Rumaysa’ (or al-Ghumaysa’) bint Milhan of Banu al-Najjar
Malik ibn al-Nadr, who refused Islam
Anas ibn Malik, the Prophet’s ﷺ servant
Carried a dagger and tended the wounded

t: Umm Sulaym accepted Islam in Madinah at the hands of Mus’ab. Her husband, Malik, was angry and left for Syria, where he died. Abu Talhah, a well-off man and a famed archer, proposed. She answered: "O Abu Talhah, do you not know that the god you worship was carved from the earth by the slave of such a tribe? Are you not ashamed to worship a tree?" He said nothing. When he proposed again, she said: "I will not marry anyone but you, but you are a disbeliever. If you become Muslim, that will be my dowry, and I will ask nothing else from you." He became Muslim and they married. Thabit said he had never heard of a dowry better than Umm Sulaym’s: Islam. (Sunan al-Nasa’i)

s.h: The night of her son’s death
t: A famous account in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Anas) tells that her son by Abu Talhah fell ill and died while Abu Talhah was out. She washed and shrouded him and laid him in a room and told the household not to tell him. When he came home, she gave him dinner and then, to the extent that a woman could, prepared herself for him. Later she said: "O Abu Talhah, if some people lent something to a family, and then asked for it back, would they be right to refuse?" He said no. She said: "Then be patient for your son." He was angry and said: "You left me until I was impure and then told me of my son?" In the morning he went to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "May Allah bless you both for your night." She conceived and gave birth to ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Talhah, whose descendants were all reciters.

At Hunayn, she was seen with a dagger tucked in her belt. Asked why, she said it was for any idolater who came near her. At Uhud, ‘A’ishah and Umm Sulaym were seen carrying water skins on their backs and pouring water into the mouths of the wounded (Sahih al-Bukhari). When her son Anas was ten, she brought him to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, he is your servant, pray for him." He prayed for his wealth and children and a long life, and Anas lived to over ninety with many children (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: Anas ibn Malik and Abu Hurayrah
The Companions rushed to stop him
"Leave him, and pour a bucket of water over it"
You were sent to make things easy

t: Anas ibn Malik reports: "A Bedouin came and urinated in a corner of the mosque. The people shouted at him. The Prophet ﷺ said: Leave him alone. When he finished, the Prophet ﷺ asked for a bucket of water and had it poured over it." (Sahih al-Bukhari). Abu Hurayrah adds the Prophet’s ﷺ words: "You were sent to make things easy, and you were not sent to make things difficult." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

In Sahih Muslim (Anas), the Prophet ﷺ called the man and said: "These mosques are not suitable for any of this urine or filth. They are only for the remembrance of Allah, prayer and the recitation of the Qur’an," or words to that effect. The man, a new Muslim, was removed from a desert life where it was normal to relieve himself anywhere. The Companions’ reaction was natural, yet it would have interrupted him mid-stream and spread impurity more widely, and humiliated a newcomer to Islam.

s.h: Why the Prophet acted this way
t: Scholars, noting the wisdom of the method, say that stopping him would have caused a greater harm (spreading the impurity over his clothes and more of the mosque), and that gentle education is a more lasting cure than shouting. It is a model of how to correct an ignorant person: let the harm be contained, remove it, and then explain.

facts: Al-Aqra’ ibn Habis al-Tamimi, a chief
"Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy"
The Prophet ﷺ carried his granddaughter Umamah while praying

t: The Prophet ﷺ kissed al-Hasan ibn ‘Ali, and al-Aqra’ ibn Habis al-Tamimi was sitting with him. Al-Aqra’ said: "I have ten children and I have never kissed any one of them." The Prophet ﷺ looked at him and said: "Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). In another narration: "What can I do if Allah has removed mercy from your heart?"

He used to pray carrying his granddaughter Umamah bint Zaynab on his shoulder: when he bowed he placed her down, and when he stood he lifted her (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). When he was giving a sermon and al-Hasan and al-Husayn came stumbling in red shirts, he came down from the pulpit, picked them up and said: "Allah spoke the truth: Your wealth and your children are but a trial. I saw these two stumbling and could not stop myself." (Sunan Abi Dawud and al-Tirmidhi). When his grandson was dying, his eyes filled with tears, and when asked, he said: "This is mercy that Allah has placed in the hearts of whom He wishes among His servants." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: She did not recognise him and said "Leave me, you have not suffered what I have"

t: The Prophet ﷺ passed by a woman who was weeping by a grave. He said to her: "Fear Allah and be patient." She said: "Go away; you have not suffered what I have suffered." She did not know him. Someone told her, "That was the Prophet ﷺ." She was overcome with remorse and came to his door, and found no guards at it. She said: "I did not recognise you." He said: "Patience is only at the first shock." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

Scholars have noted three things. First, he gave advice to a stranger in grief, and did not hold her sharp reply against her. Second, "there were no guards at his door": the leader of the Muslims was accessible to any citizen. Third, he did not ask her to stop crying; his advice was about her words and her reaction, since tears are natural. He wept himself at the death of his son Ibrahim, and said: "The eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, but we say nothing except what pleases our Lord." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah and Sahl ibn Hunayf
Scholars differ on whether standing is still recommended

t: A funeral passed in front of the Prophet ﷺ and he stood. It was said to him, "It is the funeral of a Jew." He said: "Is it not a soul?" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). In another report, Sahl ibn Hunayf and Qays ibn Sa’d were sitting in Qadisiyyah when a funeral passed; they stood. They were told it was a funeral of one of the people of the land, a non-Muslim. They said that a funeral passed in front of the Prophet ﷺ and he stood, and when told that it was a Jew, he said: "Is it not a soul?" (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Whatever the person’s faith, the sight of death is a sign of what awaits every living thing: "Is it not a soul?" Some scholars take it as an act of respect for the dead, others as a reminder of the awe of death. It shows that the Muslim community, in Madinah, lived beside people of other faiths, and the Prophet ﷺ honoured their humanity.

facts: Against the Huraqah clan of Juhaynah
Said "La ilaha illa Allah" as the sword was raised
"Did you kill him after he said La ilaha illa Allah?"
The Prophet’s ﷺ beloved, whom he later made commander

t: Usamah says: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent us in a raid against al-Huraqah of Juhaynah. We attacked them in the morning and defeated them. I and an Ansari man caught up with one of them. When we overpowered him, he said La ilaha illa Allah. The Ansari man held back, but I stabbed him with my spear and killed him. When we returned, the news reached the Prophet ﷺ, who said: O Usamah, did you kill him after he said La ilaha illa Allah? I said: O Messenger of Allah, he said it only to save himself. He said: Did you kill him after he said La ilaha illa Allah? He kept repeating it until I wished I had not accepted Islam before that day." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)
In another narration: "Did you split open his heart so that you would know whether he said it from his heart or not?" (Sahih Muslim)

Faith is judged by what people say and do, and the heart is known to Allah. A person who says the shahadah is protected. Usamah’s grief, which he carried for the rest of his life, shows how serious it was. The Prophet ﷺ later appointed him commander over an army, in his last illness, at about eighteen.

facts: Ten years, from about the age of ten
He never struck anything with his hand except in the way of Allah
"You are of a great moral character" (68:4)

t: Anas said: "I served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years. By Allah, he never said ‘uff’ to me, and he never said to me about something I did, Why did you do it? or about something I did not do, Why did you not do it?" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). In another report, he says: "The Prophet ﷺ had the best character of all people. One day he sent me on an errand. I said, By Allah, I will not go, though in my heart I intended to do as the Prophet of Allah commanded. I went out until I passed some boys playing in the market. The Prophet ﷺ seized me from behind by the neck, and I looked at him, laughing. He said: O Unays, did you go where I commanded you? I said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah, I am going." (Sahih Muslim)

‘A’ishah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant, except when fighting in the way of Allah. And he never took revenge for anything done to him, unless the limits of Allah were violated, in which case he would take revenge for the sake of Allah." (Sahih Muslim). Asked about his character, she said: "His character was the Qur’an." (Sahih Muslim)

The example shows that leadership does not require harshness. The servant was a child. The Prophet ﷺ corrected him with laughter, not with a rebuke. When Anas was an old man, he remembered the Prophet ﷺ saying: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not make people averse." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: About sixty riders of Najran, among them their bishop and leaders
In the Prophet’s mosque (as reported in the Sira)
A treaty of protection with Najran

t: In the ninth or tenth year, a delegation from the Christian city of Najran in Yemen, around sixty men including the bishop Abu Haritha and the leaders al-‘Aqib and al-Sayyid, travelled to Madinah. They came in fine robes and silk, and the Prophet ﷺ at first did not answer their greeting. When they changed to simple clothes, he did. When the time of their prayer came, the Sira reports that they started to pray in the mosque, and the Companions went to stop them; the Prophet ﷺ said: "Leave them." They prayed facing east.

They debated the nature of ‘Isa. The Prophet ﷺ recited Surah Al ‘Imran, including: "Indeed, the example of ‘Isa to Allah is like that of Adam. He created Him from dust; then He said to him, Be, and he was." (3:59) And he invited them: "Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah and not associate anything with Him and not take one another as lords instead of Allah." (3:64)

When the debate did not end, the verse of mubahalah was revealed (3:61), inviting each side to call down Allah’s curse upon the liars. The Najran delegation, after consulting each other, said, "You know he is a prophet. We will not do so" and asked for a treaty. The Prophet ﷺ agreed to protect their lives, churches and property in return for a tax, and sent with them Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, "the trustworthy one of this nation".

guides.title: The pillars of Islam and Iman
guides.blurb: The five pillars of Islam and the six articles of faith, from the hadith of Jibril.

t: To bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. A person enters Islam by saying it with understanding and sincerity.
steps.ar: أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ
steps.tl: Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah.

t: Five prayers each day at their times: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha. It is the daily link between the servant and Allah.
The obligatory charity paid by those whose savings reach the nisab and have been held for a lunar year, generally 2.5% of the wealth. It purifies wealth and supports those in need (9:60).
Fasting from dawn to sunset in the month of Ramadan, for those who are able, with understanding that the fast is also from wrongdoing in speech and action.
Visiting the Sacred House in Makkah once in a lifetime for those who are able to make the journey (3:97).
Belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree, its good and its bad. The Prophet ﷺ explained these to Jibril in the well-known hadith (Sahih Muslim).
In the same hadith, ihsan is to worship Allah as though you see Him, for even if you do not see Him, He sees you.

guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 8 (the five pillars, Ibn ‘Umar) and Sahih Muslim 8 (the hadith of Jibril, ‘Umar).

guides.title: How to make wudu
guides.blurb: The washing that prepares you for prayer, step by step.

t: Intend in your heart to make wudu for the sake of Allah, and say Bismillah. Use clean water.
Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times, right hand first.
Rinse the mouth and sniff water into the nose and blow it out, three times each.
Wash the whole face from the hairline to the chin and from ear to ear, three times. Run wet fingers through a beard.
Wash the right arm up to and including the elbow, three times, then the left arm.
Wipe over the head once with wet hands, then wipe the ears, inside with the forefingers and outside with the thumbs.
Wash the right foot up to and including the ankle, three times, then the left foot, passing the fingers between the toes.
The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever makes wudu well and then says this, the eight gates of Paradise are opened for him to enter by any he wishes (Sahih Muslim).
steps.ar: أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ
steps.tl: Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan ‘abduhu wa rasuluh.

notes: The command is in Surah al-Ma’idah (5:6): wash the face and the arms to the elbows, wipe the head, and wash the feet to the ankles.
Wudu is broken by anything that comes out of the private parts, by deep sleep, and by loss of consciousness. The schools differ on some other matters, such as touching, or eating camel meat.
Do not waste water: the Prophet ﷺ used little water for wudu.
guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 159 and Sahih Muslim 226 (the wudu of ‘Uthman, describing the Prophet ﷺ), and Surah al-Ma’idah 5:6.

guides.title: How to pray
guides.blurb: A rak’ah step by step, with the Arabic of what is recited. Small differences between the schools are noted.

t: Be in wudu, wear clean clothes that cover the awrah, and stand facing the qibla, the direction of the Ka’bah. The prayer time must have started.
Intend in your heart which prayer you are praying. Raise your hands to the shoulders or ears and say:
steps.en: Place the right hand over the left on the chest (or below the navel, in the Hanafi view).

t: Many pray this quietly before the recitation:
steps.ar: سُبْحَانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وَبِحَمْدِكَ وَتَبَارَكَ اسْمُكَ وَتَعَالَى جَدُّكَ وَلَا إِلَٰهَ غَيْرُكَ
steps.tl: Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdika wa tabarakasmuka wa ta’ala jadduka wa la ilaha ghayruk.

t: Say “A’udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim”, then Bismillah, then al-Fatihah. Reciting it is a pillar of every rak’ah in most schools.
In the first two rak’ahs of any prayer, recite a surah or some verses after al-Fatihah, for example al-Ikhlas:
Say “Allahu akbar” and bow with your back level and your hands on your knees. Then say three times:
steps.en: Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great.

t: Rise saying “Sami’a Allahu liman hamidah” and, standing, say:
Say “Allahu akbar” and go down so that the forehead and nose, both palms, both knees and the toes touch the ground. Say three times:
steps.en: Glory be to my Lord, the Most High. The Prophet ﷺ said the servant is closest to his Lord in prostration, so make dua there (Sahih Muslim).

t: Sit up saying “Allahu akbar”, and say:
steps.en: My Lord, forgive me. Then prostrate a second time as before.

steps.h: The second rak’ah and the first tashahhud
t: Stand for the second rak’ah and repeat it from al-Fatihah (without the opening supplication). In a prayer of three or four rak’ahs, sit after the second rak’ah and recite the tashahhud:
steps.ar: التَّحِيَّاتُ لِلَّهِ وَالصَّلَوَاتُ وَالطَّيِّبَاتُ، السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ، السَّلَامُ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَى عِبَادِ اللَّهِ الصَّالِحِينَ، أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ

steps.h: The final sitting: blessings on the Prophet
t: In the last rak’ah, after the tashahhud, send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ:
steps.ar: اللَّهُمَّ صَلِّ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَعَلَى آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ كَمَا صَلَّيْتَ عَلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَعَلَى آلِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ إِنَّكَ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ، اللَّهُمَّ بَارِكْ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَعَلَى آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ كَمَا بَارَكْتَ عَلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَعَلَى آلِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ إِنَّكَ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ
steps.en: You may then make any dua you wish before ending the prayer.

t: Turn your face to the right, then to the left, saying each time:

notes: Obligatory rak’ahs: Fajr 2, Dhuhr 4, Asr 4, Maghrib 3, Isha 4. Maghrib and Isha’s first two rak’ahs, and Fajr, are recited aloud; Dhuhr and Asr quietly.

The regular sunnah prayers are two before Fajr, four before and two after Dhuhr, two after Maghrib and two after Isha. The Prophet ﷺ said whoever prays twelve rak’ahs in a day, Allah builds him a house in Paradise (Sahih Muslim).
If you are learning, it is fine to start with the shortest recitations. It is better to pray imperfectly than not to pray; ask a teacher to correct you.
guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 757 (the hadith of the man who prayed badly), 6251 and Sahih Muslim (tashahhud, sujud, rak’ahs).

guides.title: Friday (Jumu’ah)
guides.blurb: How to make the most of the best day of the week.

t: Take a bath, wear your best clean clothes and perfume (for men), and go early to the mosque. The Prophet ﷺ described the reward as increasing for whoever comes earlier (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
It is recommended to read Surah al-Kahf on Friday. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does so will have a light between the two Fridays (reported by al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi).

steps.h: Send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ
t: “The best of your days is Friday; so send many blessings upon me on it” (Sunan Abi Dawud, graded sound).

steps.h: Listen to the sermon and pray
t: Two sermons are given before the prayer. Listen in silence; the prayer is two rak’ahs behind the imam. The call to it is described in Surah al-Jumu’ah:

There is an hour on Friday in which a dua is answered (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Scholars suggest it is after ‘Asr, or while the imam sits between the sermons. Be generous with dua throughout the day.

guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 881, 929 and Sahih Muslim 852; Sunan Abi Dawud 1047.

guides.title: Fasting in Ramadan
guides.blurb: What the fast is, who must fast, and how to make the most of the month.

t: Fasting Ramadan is prescribed for the believers in the verse:
Intend the next day’s fast before Fajr, in the night. Eat the pre-dawn meal (suhoor), since the Prophet ﷺ said there is blessing in it (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).

Refrain from eating, drinking and marital relations from the start of Fajr until Maghrib. Guard the tongue and the eyes: the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need of his leaving food and drink (Sahih al-Bukhari).
Break the fast as soon as the sun sets, preferably with fresh dates, or else dates or water (Sunan Abi Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, hasan). A dua reported from the Prophet ﷺ when breaking the fast:
steps.ar: ذَهَبَ الظَّمَأُ وَابْتَلَّتِ الْعُرُوقُ وَثَبَتَ الْأَجْرُ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ
steps.tl: Dhahaba az-zama’u wabtallat il-‘uruqu wa thabata al-ajru in sha’ Allah.
steps.en: The thirst has gone, the veins are moist, and the reward is confirmed, if Allah wills (Sunan Abi Dawud, hasan).

t: The sick, the traveller, women who are menstruating or with postnatal bleeding, and those for whom fasting is a serious hardship (the elderly, some pregnant or nursing women) may be excused. Those who can recover or travel make up the days later; those who cannot give a fidyah of feeding a poor person for each day (2:184). Ask a scholar for your case.
Seek Laylat al-Qadr in the odd nights of the last ten. ‘A’ishah asked the Prophet ﷺ what to say if she found it, and he told her:
steps.ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّكَ عَفُوٌّ تُحِبُّ الْعَفْوَ فَاعْفُ عَنِّي
steps.en: O Allah, You are forgiving and love forgiveness, so forgive me (Sunan at-Tirmidhi, sound).

t: At the end of Ramadan, give zakat al-fitr on behalf of yourself and your dependents before the Eid prayer: a measure of staple food for each person (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). The Prophet ﷺ encouraged fasting six days of Shawwal afterwards (Sahih Muslim).

guides.src: Surah al-Baqarah 2:183–187; Sahih al-Bukhari 1903, 1923; Sunan Abi Dawud 2357; Sunan at-Tirmidhi 3513.

guides.title: The Eid prayer and its sunnahs
guides.blurb: What to do on Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

t: Take a bath, wear your best clothes and perfume. On Eid al-Fitr, eat some dates before going out; on Eid al-Adha, it is preferred to eat after the prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sunan at-Tirmidhi).
Say the takbir on the way and until the prayer. A form reported from the Companions:
steps.ar: اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَاللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ وَلِلَّهِ الْحَمْدُ
steps.tl: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wallahu akbar, Allahu akbar, wa lillahil-hamd.

t: Two rak’ahs in congregation, without an adhan or iqamah, with extra takbirs in each rak’ah (the schools differ on their number), followed by a sermon. Everyone is encouraged to attend, including women and children (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).

Greet each other. A form reported from the Companions is “Taqabbala Allahu minna wa minkum” (may Allah accept it from us and from you). The Prophet ﷺ used to return by a different road from the one he took (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Those who are able offer an animal (udhiyah) after the prayer on the 10th of Dhul Hijjah or the three days after it, and share the meat with family and the needy. Fasting on Eid days is not permitted (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).

guides.title: How to perform Umrah
guides.blurb: The lesser pilgrimage, which can be made at any time of the year.

t: Before the miqat (the boundary point) take a bath, put on ihram clothes (two plain white sheets for men; ordinary modest clothes for women), and make the intention for Umrah, saying “Labbayka Allahumma ‘umrah”. From now on avoid the things forbidden in ihram: perfume, cutting hair or nails, covering the head (men), marital relations and hunting.
Repeat the talbiyah as you travel, men aloud:
steps.ar: لَبَّيْكَ اللَّهُمَّ لَبَّيْكَ، لَبَّيْكَ لَا شَرِيكَ لَكَ لَبَّيْكَ، إِنَّ الْحَمْدَ وَالنِّعْمَةَ لَكَ وَالْمُلْكَ، لَا شَرِيكَ لَكَ
steps.tl: Labbayka Allahumma labbayk, labbayka la sharika laka labbayk, innal-hamda wan-ni’mata laka wal-mulk, la sharika lak.

t: Enter al-Masjid al-Haram and begin at the Black Stone, with the Ka’bah on your left, circling seven times. Men uncover the right shoulder (idtiba’) and walk briskly in the first three circuits of the arrival tawaf. Between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone the Prophet ﷺ used to say:
steps.en: He also said it as his dua between those two corners (Sunan Abi Dawud, hasan).

t: After tawaf, pray two rak’ahs near the Maqam Ibrahim if you can, otherwise anywhere in the mosque. The Prophet ﷺ recited al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas in them (Sahih Muslim). Then drink Zamzam.
Go to Mount Safa. As you approach it, recite:
steps.en: Face the Ka’bah, praise Allah and make dua, then walk to Marwa. That is one lap. Complete seven laps, ending at Marwa. Men jog between the green markers.

t: Men shave the head or trim the hair; shaving is better. Women trim a fingertip’s length from the ends of their hair. Then the Umrah is complete and the restrictions of ihram end.

notes: Tawaf and sa’i can be tiring. Allow time, drink water, and be gentle with others in the crowds.
Details such as the exact placement of the miqat or what is done if a mistake is made differ in fiqh. Follow your group leader or a scholar.
guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, chapters on Hajj and Umrah; Surah al-Baqarah 2:158.

guides.title: The days of Hajj
guides.blurb: An outline of the rites, day by day. The Hajj is once in a lifetime for those who can.

t: Tamattu’: perform Umrah first, leave ihram, then enter ihram for Hajj on the 8th. Qiran: Umrah and Hajj together in one ihram. Ifrad: Hajj only. Tamattu’ and qiran require a sacrificial animal.
Enter ihram for Hajj (if in tamattu’) and go to Mina. Pray Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha and Fajr there, shortening the four-rak’ah prayers without combining them.
After sunrise go to Arafah and stay until sunset. This is the essence of the Hajj: “Hajj is Arafah” (Sunan at-Tirmidhi). Make dua at length. The best dua on this day is:
steps.ar: لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ، لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
steps.en: The Prophet ﷺ said the best dua is the dua of the Day of Arafah (Sunan at-Tirmidhi, hasan). Pray Dhuhr and Asr together, shortened, at Arafah.

t: After sunset, go to Muzdalifah without praying Maghrib on the way, then pray Maghrib and Isha together there. Spend the night, pray Fajr, make dua until it is bright, and collect pebbles for stoning.

Go to Mina and do four rites: stone Jamrat al-‘Aqabah with seven pebbles, offer the sacrifice, shave or trim the hair, and then perform Tawaf al-Ifadah at the Ka’bah (with sa’i if you are in tamattu’ or have not yet done it).
Stay at Mina and stone the three jamarat each day after noon, seven pebbles each, beginning with the smallest. You may leave on the 12th after stoning, or stay until the 13th, which is better.
Before leaving Makkah, make a final tawaf, so that the last thing you do is at the House (Sahih Muslim).

notes: Hajj is a big topic with many details. Learn from a qualified guide before you go, and rely on your group’s scholar for rulings during the journey.
The Prophet ﷺ said whoever performs Hajj and does not commit obscenity or transgression returns as on the day his mother bore him (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
guides.src: Sahih Muslim 1218 (the hadith of Jabir on the Prophet’s Hajj), and Sahih al-Bukhari, chapters on Hajj.

guides.title: The funeral prayer
guides.blurb: What to do when a Muslim dies: a community duty.

t: When news of a death reaches you, say:
steps.tl: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji’un.
steps.en: We belong to Allah and to Him we return (2:156).

t: The body is washed by Muslims of the same sex (many scholars allow a husband and wife to wash each other), then wrapped in plain white cloth. This is a community duty (fard kifayah).

It is prayed standing, with four takbirs and no bowing or prostration. After the first takbir, recite al-Fatihah; after the second, send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ as in the tashahhud; after the third, make dua for the deceased; after the fourth, pause briefly and give the salam. A dua reported from the Prophet ﷺ:
steps.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اغْفِرْ لَهُ وَارْحَمْهُ وَعَافِهِ وَاعْفُ عَنْهُ
steps.tl: Allahumma ighfir lahu warhamhu wa ‘afihi wa’fu ‘anhu.
steps.en: O Allah, forgive him, have mercy on him, give him well-being and pardon him (Sahih Muslim).

t: The deceased is buried quickly in the grave, laid on the right side facing the qibla. Those present may throw some earth into the grave and then make dua that he is kept steadfast (Sunan Abi Dawud, sound).
Bring food for the family of the deceased and visit them. Mourning is limited to three days, except for a widow, who observes four months and ten days (2:234; Sahih al-Bukhari 1280).

guides.src: Sahih Muslim 963 and Sahih al-Bukhari, chapters on funerals; Surah al-Baqarah 2:156 and 2:234.

surahIntros.1: The opening of the Book, recited in every rak’ah of the prayer. It praises Allah, affirms that He alone is worshipped and asked for help, and asks for guidance on the straight path.
surahIntros.2: The longest surah, mostly from the first years in Madinah. It lays out guidance for the believers, the story of Adam, Bani Isra’il, Ibrahim and the Ka’bah, the change of the qibla, fasting, Hajj, spending and debts, and ends with Ayat al-Kursi (255) and the last two verses.
surahIntros.3: The family of ‘Imran: the births of Maryam and ‘Isa, the oneness of Allah, and lessons from the Battle of Uhud about patience and obedience.
surahIntros.4: Rights and duties in family and community: women, orphans, inheritance, justice, and how to treat each other with fairness.
surahIntros.5: Among the last surahs revealed. It speaks of keeping covenants, lawful and unlawful food, justice, the table sent down for the disciples of ‘Isa, and the completion of the religion (5:3).
surahIntros.6: The oneness of Allah argued from His creation: the livestock, the stars of Ibrahim’s reflection, and the rejection of idol worship and false prohibitions.
surahIntros.7: The stories of Adam and Iblis and of the prophets Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, Shu’ayb and Musa, and the “heights” between Paradise and the Fire.
surahIntros.8: Revealed around the Battle of Badr: how to deal with spoils, the value of unity and steadfastness, and trust in Allah in battle.
surahIntros.9: The only surah without the Bismillah. It deals with treaties, the expedition of Tabuk, the hypocrites, and the acceptance of repentance.
surahIntros.10: Allah’s oneness and the truth of the message, the people of Yunus who believed in time, and Musa with Fir’awn.
surahIntros.11: Prophets and their peoples, with the command to stay on the right course: “So remain on a right course as you have been commanded” (11:112).
surahIntros.12: The whole surah tells the story of Yusuf, which the Qur’an calls the best of stories: jealousy, patience, temptation, prison, and forgiveness.
surahIntros.13: Thunder and the signs of Allah in nature, and the verse: “Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest” (13:28).
surahIntros.14: Ibrahim’s prayer for Makkah and his offspring, and the promise: “If you are grateful, I will surely increase you” (14:7).
surahIntros.15: The protection of the Qur’an (15:9), the people of al-Hijr, and the story of Adam and Iblis.
surahIntros.16: The bee and the many blessings of Allah, a call to gratitude, and the verse of justice and kindness recited at the end of Friday sermons (16:90).
surahIntros.17: The Night Journey, and a set of commands: kindness to parents, honesty, humility and the avoidance of waste and arrogance (17:23–39).
surahIntros.18: Four stories of trial: the people of the cave, the owner of two gardens, Musa and al-Khidr, and Dhul-Qarnayn. It is recommended to read it on Fridays.
surahIntros.19: Zakariyya and Yahya, Maryam and the birth of ‘Isa, and short accounts of Ibrahim, Musa, Isma’il and Idris.
surahIntros.20: Musa from the burning bush to the confrontation with Fir’awn, the story of Adam, and a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.
surahIntros.21: The prophets as one community with one message: Musa, Ibrahim, Lut, Nuh, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya and Maryam.
surahIntros.22: The call to Hajj raised by Ibrahim, the rites and their meaning, and the first permission to defend against oppression (22:39).
surahIntros.23: The qualities of the successful believers, the stages of human creation, and the messengers who came before.
surahIntros.24: The Verse of Light (35), the manners of the home and community, lowering the gaze, and the false accusation against ‘A’ishah.
surahIntros.25: The Qur’an as the criterion between right and wrong, and the portrait of the servants of the Most Merciful (25:63–76).
surahIntros.26: Prophets and their peoples told with a repeated refrain: Musa, Ibrahim, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu’ayb.
surahIntros.27: The ant, Sulayman and the Queen of Sheba, and the stories of Salih, Lut and Musa.
surahIntros.28: The story of Musa from his birth to Madyan and back to Egypt, and the arrogant wealth of Qarun.
surahIntros.29: The spider’s house as an image of weak refuge, and the reminder that faith is tested through trials.
surahIntros.30: The Romans, signs of Allah in creation and love between spouses (30:21), and the call to turn to the upright religion.
surahIntros.31: Luqman’s advice to his son: no partner with Allah, kindness to parents, prayer, patience and humility.
surahIntros.32: The creation of the heavens, earth and humankind, the Day of Resurrection, and the rewards of those who rise at night to pray.
surahIntros.33: The Battle of the Trench, the household of the Prophet ﷺ, the rules of modesty, and the statement that he is the Seal of the Prophets (33:40).
surahIntros.34: Dawud and Sulayman, the people of Saba and their ungrateful end, and the certainty of resurrection.
surahIntros.35: Allah as the Originator of the heavens and earth, and the verse: “Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge” (35:28).
surahIntros.36: The Qur’an’s call to the Hereafter, the messengers sent to a town, and the signs of Allah’s power over death and life.
surahIntros.37: The ranks of angels, and the stories of Nuh, Ibrahim and the sacrifice of his son, Musa and Harun, Ilyas, Lut and Yunus.
surahIntros.38: Dawud, Sulayman and Ayyub, the story of Adam and Iblis, and the contrast between the pious and the transgressors.
surahIntros.39: Sincere worship of Allah alone, the groups led to Paradise and the Fire, and the verse of hope: “Do not despair of the mercy of Allah” (39:53).
surahIntros.40: Allah as the Forgiver of sin, and the believing man of Fir’awn’s household who defended Musa.
surahIntros.41: The Qur’an explained in Arabic, the signs in creation, and the advice to repel evil with what is better (41:34).
surahIntros.42: Consultation as a trait of the believers, the nature of revelation, and the verse: “There is nothing like Him” (42:11).
surahIntros.43: Ornaments and worldly show, Ibrahim’s declaration of faith, Musa and ‘Isa, and the Hereafter’s friendships.
surahIntros.44: The Qur’an revealed in a blessed night, the warning of a day of smoke, and the fate of Fir’awn.
surahIntros.45: The signs in the heavens and earth, the people who kneel on the Day of Judgment, and the record of deeds.
surahIntros.46: The people of ‘Ad and their sand dunes, the jinn who listened to the Qur’an, and the dua of one who reaches forty (46:15).
surahIntros.47: Fighting in defence, steadfastness, the hypocrites, and reflecting on the Qur’an. It names the Prophet ﷺ directly.
surahIntros.48: The victory and peace after Hudaybiyyah, the pledge under the tree, and the calm sent down on the believers’ hearts.
surahIntros.49: The manners of a community: respect for the Prophet ﷺ, checking news, avoiding mockery and backbiting, and the verse: “The most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous” (49:13).
surahIntros.50: Resurrection and the two angels who record, and the reminder that Allah is nearer than the jugular vein (50:16).
surahIntros.51: The winds, the guests of Ibrahim, and the statement that humans and jinn were created to worship Allah (51:56).
surahIntros.52: Mount Tur, the Day of Judgment, and the reward of the believers and their families.
surahIntros.53: The Prophet’s vision of Jibril and his ascent, and the call to bow and prostrate at the end.
surahIntros.54: The splitting of the moon, the destruction of earlier peoples, and the refrain: “We have made the Qur’an easy for remembrance.”
surahIntros.55: Allah’s blessings in creation and the Hereafter, with the refrain: “So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?”
surahIntros.56: The Event of the Day of Judgment and the three groups of people: the foremost, the companions of the right and the left.
surahIntros.57: Iron as a symbol of strength, the call to spend in Allah’s cause, and the true value of this worldly life (57:20).
surahIntros.58: The woman (Khawlah) who pleaded with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband, and the manners of gatherings and private counsel.
surahIntros.59: The exile of Banu Nadir, and the closing verses that list many of the Names of Allah.
surahIntros.60: The woman who is tested, the example of Ibrahim, and how to treat those who did not fight the believers.
surahIntros.61: The ranks: believers should act on what they say, and ‘Isa gave glad tidings of a messenger named Ahmad (61:6).
surahIntros.62: The Friday prayer: respond to the call and leave trade, then spread through the land and remember Allah much.
surahIntros.63: The traits of the hypocrites, and the warning that wealth and children should not distract from remembering Allah.
surahIntros.64: The Day of Mutual Loss and Gain, and the reminder that spouses and children can be a trial.
surahIntros.65: The rules of divorce and the waiting period, with repeated calls to taqwa: “Whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out” (65:2).
surahIntros.66: A matter in the Prophet’s household, repentance, and Maryam and Asiya as examples for believers.
surahIntros.67: The sovereignty of Allah, the creation of death and life as a test, and reflection on the heavens. The Prophet ﷺ said it intercedes for its reader (Sunan at-Tirmidhi).
surahIntros.68: The pen, the Prophet’s great character (68:4), and the lesson of the owners of the garden.
surahIntros.69: The Inevitable Reality, the fate of ‘Ad, Thamud and Fir’awn, and the truth of the Qur’an.
surahIntros.70: The stairways of ascent, patience, and the qualities of those who are saved: prayer, charity and trustworthiness.
surahIntros.71: Nuh’s long call to his people, his dua, and its outcome.
surahIntros.72: The jinn who heard the Qur’an and believed, and the Prophet’s duty to convey.
surahIntros.73: The wrapped one: the command to rise at night, recite the Qur’an in measured tones, and bear a weighty word.
surahIntros.74: The cloaked one: an early command to rise and warn, to glorify his Lord, purify his clothes and be patient.
surahIntros.75: Resurrection, the fingertips Allah can restore, and the moment of death.
surahIntros.76: The human being, and the righteous who give food to the needy, orphan and captive for Allah’s sake alone (76:8).
surahIntros.77: The winds sent forth, with the repeated warning: “Woe that Day to the deniers.”
surahIntros.78: The Great News of resurrection, the Day of Decision, and the signs of Allah’s power.
surahIntros.79: Those who pull out souls, the confrontation of Musa and Fir’awn, and the coming of the Hour.
surahIntros.80: He frowned: a gentle correction when the blind man ‘Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum came to the Prophet ﷺ, and a reminder that the Qur’an is for all who fear Allah.
surahIntros.81: The folding up of the sun and the signs of the Last Day, and the truth of the Qur’an as the word of a noble messenger.
surahIntros.82: The cleaving of the heavens, and the angels who record every deed.
surahIntros.83: A warning against cheating in weights and measures, and the picture of the sinners and the righteous in the Hereafter.
surahIntros.84: The splitting of the sky, and the book of deeds taken in the right hand or from behind. It has a verse of prostration.
surahIntros.85: The oath by the constellations and the story of the People of the Ditch who were persecuted for their belief.
surahIntros.86: The night comer, the creation of humankind, and the Qur’an as a decisive word.
surahIntros.87: Glorify your Lord, the Most High. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite it in the Friday and Eid prayers and in Witr (Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud).
surahIntros.88: The overwhelming Day, Paradise and the Fire, and a call to look at the camel, the sky, the mountains and the earth.
surahIntros.89: The dawn, the fates of ‘Ad, Thamud and Fir’awn, and the call to the tranquil soul to return to its Lord.
surahIntros.90: The city of Makkah, and the steep path: freeing a slave, feeding in a time of hunger, being among those who believe and enjoin patience.
surahIntros.91: The sun and the soul: whoever purifies it has succeeded, and whoever corrupts it has failed.
surahIntros.92: The night, and two paths: one who gives and fears Allah, and one who is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient.
surahIntros.93: The morning brightness: Allah’s reassurance to the Prophet ﷺ, and His command to care for the orphan and the beggar.
surahIntros.94: The opening of the chest and the promise: “So, surely with hardship comes ease” (94:5–6).
surahIntros.95: The fig and the olive, and the creation of the human being in the best of forms.
surahIntros.96: The first five verses revealed to the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira: “Read in the name of your Lord who created.”
surahIntros.97: The Night of Power, which is better than a thousand months.
surahIntros.98: The clear evidence, and the call to sincere worship of Allah, prayer and zakat.
surahIntros.99: The earthquake of the Last Day, and the accounting of even an atom’s weight of good or evil.
surahIntros.100: The charging horses, and a reproach to the human who is ungrateful to his Lord.
surahIntros.101: The Striking Calamity, the weighing of deeds, and the heavy and light scales.
surahIntros.102: The competition in wealth and numbers that keeps people from the Hereafter until the grave.
surahIntros.103: Time: all of humankind is in loss, except those who believe, do good, and advise each other to truth and patience.
surahIntros.104: A warning against the one who slanders and hoards wealth.
surahIntros.105: The story of Abraha’s army with its elephant, which was destroyed in the year the Prophet ﷺ was born.
surahIntros.106: The security Allah gave Quraysh in their trade journeys, and the call to worship the Lord of this House.
surahIntros.107: The one who denies the Judgment, harshly pushes away the orphan and does not encourage feeding the poor, and the heedless in prayer.
surahIntros.108: The shortest surah: the abundance Allah gave to the Prophet ﷺ, and the command to pray and sacrifice for Him.
surahIntros.109: A clear declaration of worship: “For you is your religion, and for me is my religion.”
surahIntros.110: The help of Allah and the conquest, and the command to glorify and seek forgiveness. It was among the last revealed.
surahIntros.111: The fate of Abu Lahab, an uncle of the Prophet ﷺ who opposed him.
surahIntros.112: The oneness of Allah in four verses. The Prophet ﷺ said it equals a third of the Qur’an (Sahih al-Bukhari).
surahIntros.113: Seeking refuge with the Lord of daybreak from evil. The Prophet ﷺ recited it with the next surah before sleeping (Sahih al-Bukhari).
surahIntros.114: Seeking refuge with the Lord of mankind from the whisperer who withdraws when Allah is remembered.
